title: 2013B Question 4
text:
Question
Discuss the physiological significance of the blood-brain barrier.

title: 2013B Question 4
text:
Suggested Structure
Discuss how the barrier’s structural and transport properties support each physiological function, including the significance of regions without a barrier.


Structure and Selective Permeability


Neuronal Homeostasis and Protection


Circumventricular Organs


Altered Barrier Function

title: 2013B Question 4
text:
Examiner Comments

38.9% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
Candidates were expected to include a definition of the blood brain barrier (BBB) and the micro-anatomical features, unique to its function. The control of ion passage, along with which substances could freely pass and those which cannot was expected. Description of how the area postrema lies outside the BBB and the role in emesis was considered to be basic knowledge; better answers included other circumventricular organs and their role.
Many candidates incorrectly believed gap junctions to be present. Knowledge of neuroanatomy, and location of various physiological control centres within the brain was generally poor when specified in answers.
Most candidates correctly identified the role of the BBB in neuronal homeostasis, and the protective function against pathogens and toxins. Better answers included a barrier function separating central neurotransmitters from the periphery and vice versa, including descriptions of enzyme systems.
There was a wide variation in answers as to which ions were able to pass the blood brain barrier and which were not. Most candidates correctly identified the impermeability to proteins. The role of carbon dioxide in altering CSF pH, with ensuing stimulation of the respiratory centre was generally well understood when described. Many candidates discussed Fick’s law of diffusion. Very few candidates were able to correctly interpret how it applied to the selective permeability of the BBB.
Many candidates also described the Monro-Kellie doctrine relating to intracranial pressure, which was not considered relevant to the actual question.
Better answers also included situations of altered function of the BBB (neonate, meningitis, profound hypertension etc). When describing particular properties of the BBB, examples of drugs (in particular those commonly used in anaesthesia) relating to those properties was useful.

title: 2013B Question 4
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
The Blood brain barrier is a physiological barrier that prevents free movement of substances  between ECF of the body and the ECF of the CNS. 
The BBB is composed of:

Capillary endothelial cells joined with tight junctions
Basement Membrane 
Astrocytes (Glial Cells) with extended foot processes that further reduce permeability
Transporters 

GLUT-1
Ion Channels (Ca, Na, K)
Enzymes (MAO, AChE) prevent circulating neurotransmitters from entering brain
Factors affecting permeability
Fick’s law of diffusion: (ΔP.A.k)/T
k= Lipid Solubility/Sq MW → ↑ lipid solubility / ↓MW → ↑ permeability 
Not protein bound
Not ionised
Non Polar 
Freely permeable: 
H20
Very low MW: O2, COW
Very Lipid Soluble: Propofol, ketones 
Circumventricular organs 
Due to sensing functions several areas exist outside the BBB, these are called the Circumventricular organs 

Area postrema –  also known as the chemoreceptor trigger zone; responsible for sensing noxious substances in the peripheral circulation → rigger nausea ± vomiting when detected
Organum Vasculosum Laminae Terminalis (OVLT) – contains osmoreceptors directly in contact with peripheral circulation sends signal to release ADH in response to ↑osmolality
Subfornical Organ (SFO) – contains osmoreceptors as well as glucose sensors! senses energy state of the body
Posterior pituitary – releases ADH and oxytocin into the circulation
Pineal gland – responsible for regulating circadian rhythm via release of melatonin

Functions of the BBB:

Maintain a stable extracellular environment - preventing fluctuation in electrolyte levels and pH 

BBB maintains a stable pH as it is relatively impermeable to H+/OH- ions
CO2 freely diffuses across BBB → dissociates to H+ and HCO3– 
→ alters CSF pH ∴ medullary respiratory centre uses CSF pH as a surrogate marker for PaCO2, which is a reflection of adequacy of ventilation

Protection of the brain from toxins and immune system

BBB protects brain from:

pathogens in blood (damaged BBB → encephalitis)
the body’s immune system (damaged BBB → autoimmune reaction to exposed CNS tissue; e.g. multiple sclerosis)

BBB leakiness in neonate brain exposed to unconjugated bilirubin (which is neurotoxic)

Protection of the body from CNS neurotransmitters.

The BBB contains various enzymes (e.g. MAO, AChE, etc) which degrade neurotransmitters and prevent their passage across BBB

title: 2013B Question 5

Examiner Comments

28.7% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
There was significant variation across candidates in interpretation of the question. The highest scoring answers were able to concentrate on water and the kidney, while not getting distracted by concepts such as baroreceptors, and the role of the autonomic nervous system. To score good marks it was necessary to describe in some detail the handling of water by the kidney at the various points along the nephron. Curiously however, even the lowest scoring answers usually clearly and correctly described the role of V2 receptors and aquaporin channels in the collecting duct. Long introductory paragraphs were frequent but almost never constructive in terms of gaining marks, and only served to waste valuable time. Similarly, there is no point in duplicating information contained in a diagram with text and vice versa. A significant number of otherwise good answers omitted to mention the production of urine as the end result of all this, and the important fact that diuresis can be osmotically variable.

Passing Standard
Kidneys have an important role in regulating total body waster and osmolality by altering urine volume and its make up.
Renal Blood flow and Filtration:

Renal blood flow: 1440l/day 
Glomerular filtration rate: 180l/day, this is regulated / maintained over a broad range of MAP (~70-170mmHg) by myogenic auto regulation and tubuloglomerular feedback. 
myogenic mechanism – ↑RPP → afferent arteriole stretch → reflex contraction! ↓RBP ! ↓GFR
Tubuloglomerular feedback →↑GFR →↑filtered NaCl → sensed by macula densa →↑adenosine →↓GFR

The kidneys regulate urine production from between 500ml to many L with an osmolality range from 40-1400mOsm .
Renal fluid management by location:
Proximal Convoluted tubule:

The proximal tubule reabsorbs 60% of filtrate (water) including electrolytes and filtered products
Reabsorption unregulated 

Descending (thin) Loop of Henle

Thin descending limb is permeable to water so further water reabsorption  ~15% 

Thick (ascending) loop of Henle and Distal converted tubule 

Impervious to water, active reabsorption of solute through Na/K/2Cl cotransporter establishes the concentration gradient for urine concentration in the collecting duct.

Distal convoluted tubule 

Macula densa in proximal DCT detects Na concentration from increased/decreased flow rates → regulation of afferent arteriole blood flow, and in low flow states stimulates release of rennin from JG cells → Activation of RAAS pathway 
Small amount of water reabsorption following 3Na/2K ATPase pump activity regulated by aldosterone

Collecting Duct 

Urine concentration through ADH acting on V2 rectors → inserting aquaporin into lumen cell surface can reabsorb further ~15% of urine 

CD is the primary site of urine concentration when required.
Renal Water Regulation: 
Auto regulation through myogenic and tubuloglmerular feedback
Renin release → Angiotensin I → Angiotensin II → Aldosterone 
Renin 
Tubuloglomerular mechanism and Beta 1 adrenergic stimulation → ↑ renin release 
Angiotensin II: 

↑fluid and NaCl reabsorption, ↑ECF volume
ADH release 
thirst

↑ thirst
↑ water reabsorption and concentrated urine formation

title: 2013B Question 6
text:
Examiner Comments

40.1% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
In general, the key points that attracted the majority of marks included:

an accurate description of the structure of haemoglobin
the sites of haemoglobin breakdown
an explanation of the subsequent metabolism of iron, haem and globin
the fate of iron released during haem metabolism
the pathway of haem breakdown - into biliverdin and then bilirubin, transport of bilirubin to the liver, conjugation of bilirubin, and subsequent excretion in bile
a description and explanation of enterohepatic circulation
ultimately excretion of urobilinogen and stercobilinogen

Better answers often included a well labelled diagram and explanatory notes that further demonstrated understanding of each stage of haemoglobin metabolism. Extra marks were awarded for a description of proteins and enzymes involved in the metabolic pathways, mentioning the production of carbon monoxide due to haem metabolism, demonstrating understanding of the significance of bilirubin conjugation, and the function of the breakdown products. Common errors included – poor (and often incorrect) description of haemoglobin structure, long descriptions of haemoglobin and red cell function (which did not attract marks), incorrect descriptions and a lack of understanding of the haem metabolic pathways, and not discussing iron or globin metabolism.

title: 2013B Question 6
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Haemoglobin
Haemoglobin serve a primary function in the transport of O2 and CO2 and acid base balance. 
They have no nucleus or mitochondria and are biconcave disc shape.  
Haemoglobin comprises 4 subunits , each having one polypeptide chain and one heme group

Polypeptide chains - globin, in audits primarily 2 alpha, 2 beta
Haem groups with contain a porphyrin ring with central Iron (Fe2+)

Haemoglobin Metabolism:
Haemoglobin have a life span of approx. 120 days. They are broken down through:

Loss of flexibility (age related) in small capillaries of the Reticuloendothelial system where they phagocytosed in the spleen (major mechanism), liver, and bone marrow 
Haemolysis (approx. 10%) in circulation 

Haemoglobin is broken down (lysis) into its constant parts 

Globin: Degraded by proteases → amino acids → maybe recycled into new protein production
Heme broken down by Haemoxygenase to Iron Fe2+ and Biliverdin 
Iron: Fe2+ bound with apoferritin → Ferritin → for transported for storage or formation of new Hb
Biliverdin:

biliverdin → reduced to unconjugated bilirubin (biliverdin reductase) → transported bound to albumin to the liver 

Bilirubin conjugated in the liver to conjugated bilirubin → water soluble → secreted in bile to the  GIT

In GIT bacteria metabolise Bilirubin to Urobilinogen which may then 



→ 18% undergo enterohepatic circulation and be reabsorbed and re excreted in bile
→ 80% undergo further metabolism by GIT bacteria to stercobilinogen → excretion in faeces
→ 2% undergoes enterohepatic recirculation and urinary excretion, where it is oxidised to urobilin

i.e. spleen red pulp, lymph nodes

title: 2013B Question 7
text:
Examiner Comments

38.9% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
Good answers were well organized with a concise introductory heading followed by classification into metabolic, immunological, haematological, musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, foetal, vascular and permissive effects.
Some good answers included a description of mechanism of action of cortisol at the molecular level, which gained extra marks. Similarly, candidates who were able to explain why cortisol is a “stress hormone” and what benefits it confer to the individual scored extra marks. A few well-written answers also included a discussion of how cortisol exerts its anti-inflammatory effects.
Many candidates mentioned osteoporosis as a physiologic effect when in fact it occurs only in conditions of excess glucocorticoids over long periods.
Irrelevant to the question are:

Circadian nature of ACTH secretion, which is the cause of confusion to many candidates. (Cortisol is NOT the hormone responsible for normal sleep-awake cycle)
Regulatory control of cortisol and the negative feedback loop. (However, marks were awarded to candidates who mentioned that glucocorticoids inhibit ACTH secretion)
A system-based description of Cushing syndrome, which is a pathological state.
Steroid supplementation during surgery.

The main cause for failing this question was insufficient detail demonstrating a lack of knowledge and poor understanding.

Passing Standard
Glucocorticoids are steroid hormones the act on intracellular receipts to alter protein production from DNA.  The primary endogenous glucocorticoid is cortisol produced in the Zona Fasciculata of the adrenal cortex. 
Cortisol is released in a diurnal pattern and regulated by CRH→ACTH release in the hypothalamus and pituitary. It’s also released in response to stress and hypoglycaemia. 
Exogenous glucocorticoids include hydrocortisone, prednisolone and dexamethasone. 
Physiological effects of glucocorticoids include:

Overall ↑plasma glucose, lipid and ketone body levels 

Inhibition of glucose uptake in the muscle and adipose tissue 
Increases glycogenolysis 
Stimulates gluconeogenesis, particularly in the liver

↑ risk of infection

Measurement System and Natural Frequency

Underdamped, Overdamped and Optimally Damped Tracings

title: 2013B Question 8
text:
Examiner Comments

30.6% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
A brief description of an invasive arterial blood pressure measurement system followed by a definition of resonance and a definition of damping allowed for better structuring of answers. What was required after that was a slightly more detailed description of why resonance could be an issue and how it is engineered out of the measurement system. A discussion of the range of values for damping that could apply to a system and what those values mean, followed by an appreciation of critical and optimal damping would round out a good answer.
The most common reason for not passing this question was simply being too brief and not including enough of the elements that were expected in an answer to this question. Repetition of material was present in many answers but was not rewarded with additional credit. More than a few answers confused critical and optimal damping with the range of values given for optimal damping falling between 0.33 and 0.8. Better answers demonstrated a methodical approach to the question, had accurate drawings and were factually correct.

title: 2013B Question 8
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Arterial blood pressure may be monitored invasively using an arterial cannula connected through hydraulic coupling to a pressure transducer.
Arterial pressure oscillations transmitted → arterial line-tube-fluid column setup → pressure transducer → converted to an electric signal
Accuracy of pressure transduction through the equipment/apparatus are influenced by resonance and dampening. 
Natural Frequency
Natural frequency is the frequency a system tends to oscillate around in the absence of any driving or dampening force.
Resonance
Resonance is the phenomenon  for system to oscillate at increased  amplitude in the presence of a system or force of similar frequency - resonant frequency. 
If the natural frequency of an arterial line system matches the natural frequency of the arterial oscillation (pulsation) → resonance → amplification of oscillations → waveform reading inaccuracy.
If a pulse range required to be measure if from 30-180bpm → 0.5-3Hz. The arterial line natural frequency must be approx. 8x higher ~24Hz to avoid resonance occurring. 
Usually, the natural frequency of the arterial line setup is designed to be ≈ 200 Hz but a number of factors may reduce this:

↑ Tubing Diameter / ↓ Tube Length →↑Natural Frequency
Air in the line →↓natural frequency 
↓Compliance →↑Natural Frequency

Consequences of ↑resonance in the measuring system: 

falsely elevated systolic arterial pressure
falsely reduced diastolic arterial pressure
mean arterial pressure relatively unaffected

Damping
Damping is the tendency of a system to resist oscillations via dissipation of energy.

Overdamped system will rapidly stop oscillations 
Underdamped system will very slowly stop oscillations 
Undamped system will continue to oscillate indefinitely

Factors that ↑damping: 

kinked tubing
↑compliance of tubing
↑length of tubing
blood clot in tubing
air bubble in tubing

Consequences of overdamping:

underestimate SBP
overestimate DBP
MAP relatively unaffected
loss of details of arterial pressure oscillation e.g. lost dicrotic notch





Prize

List:

Arterial line: components, how it works, accuracy
Physics of SHM: definitions
Dynamic accuracy



Arterial line:








Components

Cannula with anti-clot
Compressible tubing with saline
Pressure transducer: diaphragm with four strain gauges (conductor)
Saline bag under pressure
1-3mL/h infusion and ability to flush
Electronic display



Function

Continuous column between arterial blood and transducer
↑↓ oscillations in pressure → displacement of diaphragm → stretch/relax strain gauges → ↑/↓ electrical resistance → amplification → arterial trace
Accuracy improved by multiple strain gauges +/- Wheatstone bridge



Accuracy
Static:

Zero relative to atmospheric pressure
Time calibration: observe steadiness at zero
Height calibration: e.g. move transducer against a standard

Dynamic:

Optimise damping
Minimise resonance







Physics of simple harmonic motion:








Natural frequency (FN)

Definition: tendency of a system once disturbed to oscillate at a particular frequency about its equilibrium position.
Determinants: FN ∝ potential energy (stiffness) / kinetic energy (mass)

Potential energy ∝ tube elastance x diaphragm elastance
Kinetic energy ∝ (length x tube compliance x density) / (radius)




Fundamental frequency (F0)

Lowest frequency oscillation within a system (e.g. heart rate in ABP trace)



Resonance

Definition: where repeated disturbance of a system at its natural frequency (or at a close multiple of it) causes increasing amplitude of oscillation
Effect on ABP trace: ↑SBP, ↓DBP, ↔︎mAP, contributes to peripheral dicrotic notch



Damping

Definition: minimization of oscillatory amplitude through viscous and frictional forces
Equation: damping ∝ (Length x volume of displacement x viscosity) / (diameter x density)
Damping coefficient: index of rate of decay of oscillations
Optimal damping: balance between maximizing response speed and minimizing overshoot
Effect on ABP trace: ↓SBP, ↑DBP, ↔︎mAP, delayed waveform, loss of high frequency components e.g. incisura








To ensure dynamic accuracy:








Minimise resonance
Aim:

FN ≥ 10x F0 hence resonance unlikely to occur
Flat frequency response at or near the measured frequencies
No exaggeration of amplitude of measured frequencies

Means:

↑potential energy (stiffness): non-compliant tubing and diaphragm
↓ kinetic energy: short, wide, non-compliant tubing and low density fluid



Optimise damping
Aim:

Flat frequency response up to 2/3 of FN
Minimal phase distortion i.e. minimal and more homogenous lag
Damping coefficient 0.64
Exactly two oscillations after fast flush test
<7% overshoot overall
<2% overshoot for harmonics (if Fourier analysis performed)

Means:

Intact cannula, no kink, no clot, no bubbles
System design



Graph

*Note: modern systems are underdamped, but natural frequency is high enough to obviate resonance*

title: 2013B Question 9

Suggested Structure

title: 2013B Question 9
text:
Examiner Comments

28% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
Good answers started with the principles and then explained how cephazolin was an appropriate choice for antibiotic chemoprophylaxis for joint replacement.
The principles included discussion on the bacteria that the antibiotic is trying to prevent infection from (mainly gram positive skin commensals for a joint replacement), noting that this was not treatment for an established infection. Good answers also described the need to alter the antibiotic if the patient had established or was at risk for methicillin resistant staphlococcus.
Many candidates did not know cephazolin is a first generation cephalosporin with good bactericidal effect on gram positive cocci. Better candidates explained how prevention was not necessary for all “clean” surgery but circumstances such as implants having high morbidity from infection had led to the guidelines for prevention. The appropriate timing and dosage of the antibiotic for optimal tissue penetration prior to skin incision, the duration of therapeutic effect and the requirements to repeat the dose if the surgery is prolonged were important concepts to explain. Also relevant was the need to limit the development of resistance by selection of the antibiotic and not prolonging its use. Antibiotics chosen for prophylaxis need to have a high therapeutic index and minimal side effects. Cost should be low.
Please note that loose terminology such as “bugs” and “orthopods” are not of an acceptable standard for this written examination.

title: 2013B Question 9
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Antibiotic chemoprophylaxis is the principle of using antibiotics to prevent surgical site infections, morbidity and mortality.
General Principles:

Assess risk of infection and need for prophylaxis (clean, contaminated, dirty surgery and patient factors/ comorbidities), clean surgery does not routinely require prophylaxis, not for treatment of infection. 
Select the ideal agent and use in an appropriate way
Work against the pathogens most likely to contaminate site, with consideration of their resistance patterns 
Shortest effective durations 
Correct administration to ensure optimal concentration during the procedure 
Minimal adverse effects 
Adverse drug reaction from the antibiotic 
Selection pressure for resistant organisms
Complications (such as Clostridium difficile infections and cannula site infections) 

Cephazolin in joint replacement as an example:

Risk of infection moderate however morbidity associated with infection high as impacting prothesis into bone so antibiotic chemoprophylaxis indicated 
Infection most likely from skin commensals including staphylococcal and streptococcal bacteria. 
First generation cephalosporins (i.e. cephazolin) effective against skin commensal gram positive cocci, antibiotic child by be changed/influenced by presence or likelihood of resistant organisms i.e. MRSA
Cephazolin is bactericidal
Cephazolin IV formulation ideal for rapid delivery and absorption.  
Dosage of cephazolin (25mg/kg) at least 15min but no longer than 60min prior to knife from skin / tourniquet inflation. 
Duration 4 hours, repeat dose required in longer cases.

Yes

(Note gram negative rods common in hospitalized patients)

title: 2013B Question 11

Examiner Comments

31.8% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
It was expected that candidates would explain how the NSAIDS block cyclo-oxygenase enzymes, that there were two iso-enzymes and their bodily distribution and function. The mechanisms of how they produce their wanted effects were expected i.e. in reducing pain, inflammation and pyrexia.
Most candidates indicated the advantages of the COX-2 agents i.e. minimal gastric erosions, less bleeding and less alteration of renal blood flow auto regulation. Some did not realise that bronchoconstriction in asthmatics is also minimalised. Most candidates had mentioned the major disadvantage. This is increasing the balance of prostaglandins towards thrombosis in at risk patients.
Those candidates that did not score well did not elaborate sufficiently or did not answer part of the question.

title: 2013B Question 11
text:

    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize

Passing Standard
NSAIDS are used to treat pain and act via inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase enzyme pathways to decrease prostaglandins. 
COX enzymes function to convert arachidonic acid → Prostaglandins.
There are 2 primary COX enzymes:
COX1: is physiological and important for haemostatic function and in platelets, induces platelet aggregation through production of thromboxane A2. 
COX 2: COX2 expression is induced with tissue damage 
NSAIDs can be either 

Nonselective - Irreversible: e.g. Aspirin
Nonselective - Reversible: e.g. Ibuprofen, naproxen
Selective COX2: celecoxib, parecoxib

Clinical effects of NSAIDS:
Analgesia and Anti-inflammatory 
Inhibition of prostaglandin production as sites of injury →↓ in stimulation of pain transduction from stimulation of prostanoid receptors, decrease in positive feedback inflammatory mediator release.  
Anti-pyrexial effect  via inhibiting PGE2 action centrally 
Antiplatelet effect due to inhibition of COX 1 →↓thromboxane A2 production
NSAID Side Effects:
CVS: ↑ risk Thrombotic events from COX2 specific agents, selective COX 2 inhibition → increased Thromboxane  A2(from COX1) : PGI2 ratio → increased risk of thrombosis
Resp: Asthma/Bronchospasm,  ↓ cox mediated arachnoid acid → prostaglandin pathway →↑ leukotriene production  
Haem: Inhibition
GI: inhibition of PGE2, PGI2 production →↓pH/ ↑Acid production, diminished mucus secretion → dyspepsia, ↑risk of ulceration → GI Bleed
Renal: Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole, NSAIDs decrease renal blood flow through inhibition of PGE2, PGI2 production → decreased afferent arteriolar dilation
Advantages and Disadvantages of Selective COX2 Inhibition
 Advantages
↓Risk of peptic ulcer disease
↓Platelet dysfunction
↓ alteration in renal blood flow autoregulation 
↓rate of bronchospasm 
Disadvantages
 Usu. more expensive
 Can also precipitate acute kidney injury
 ↑Risk of thrombosis – e.g. myocardial infarct, stroke, etc through increased Thromboxane  A2(from COX1) : PGI2 ratio → increased risk of thrombosis

Examiner Comments

24.8% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
This question calls for an explanation of how these two drugs are used based on their comparative pharmacokinetics. Failure to link the pharmacokinetics with the usage resulted in low marks. Discussion of non-intravenous routes of administration was not a productive strategy.

title: 2013B Question 13

Examiner Comments

38.9% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
This question requires a good understanding and application of pharmacodynamics as relate to muscle relaxants.
Graphs with log dose on the horizontal axis are more conventional; some graphs included the log dose on the vertical axis. Provided the shape of the graph was different and reflected the relationship to response (percent depression of single twitch in a graded graph or percentage of respondents satisfying a criterion e.g. 95 percent twitch height depression) marks were allocated accordingly.
The most complete graphs included the following discussions;

Explanations for the three phases of the graph, the first horizontal , the steep, and the final horizontal component in terms of the interaction of rocuronium with the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
Important intercepts such as the 95 % single twitch suppression response in a graded graph and the ED 95 in a quantal graph
Factors that affect the steepness of the slope in any given individual such as interindividual variability in response

Discussions about graded and quantal curves were important as were the definition of ED95, being an important prelude to answering the second part of the question where factors were influencing the apparent value of the ED 95.
The second part of the question was better answered. Candidates recognised, listed and often described mechanisms for the factors altering the curves.
There was some confusion as to whether rocuronium should be considered an “agonist” or “antagonist” for the purposes of discussing agents that oppose its effects such as anticholinesterases and sugammadex.

title: 2013B Question 14
text:
Examiner Comments

38.9% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
To pass the question, candidates were required to recognise that drugs could both increase and decrease uterine tone. They were also required to list at least five or six drugs which affected uterine tone and provide an accurate outline of their side effect profiles. Drugs that increase uterine tone, which earned marks, were: oxytocin derivatives; ergot alkaloids; and prostaglandins (PGE2, PGE1 and PGF2α). Tocolytic drugs which scored marks were: NSAIDS; dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (nifedipine); nitrates; Β2 agonists; volatile anaesthetic agents; magnesium; and oxytocin receptor antagonists. Extra credit was awarded for including more drugs, with side effect profiles, from the above list. Marks were also awarded for realising that all oxytocics pose a risk of uterine rupture and foetal compromise if given prior to delivery. Similarly, credit was given for mention that tocolytics increase the risk of post partum haemorrhage. There were a few excellent answers.
Common sources of error included incorrect details of the side effects of these classes of drugs, especially the haemodynamic consequences of oxytocics. Many candidates did not mention the possibility of ADH like effects with oxytocin, which although uncommon, do need to be borne in mind when delivering the drug as an infusion for induction of labour. Another common misbelief was that nifedipine causes bradycardia, rather than a reflex tachycardia. The haemodynamic effects of magnesium (which occur at high plasma concentrations) also tended to be overstated at the expense of more common side effects. This may have been because many answers classified magnesium as an “effective calcium channel blocker”. A host of drugs, having no effect on uterine tone, were also given.
Many candidates gave lengthy discussions on the mechanism of action, dosing regimen and specific indications for the drugs, which would have used valuable time and did not attract any marks.

title: 2013B Question 15
text:
Examiner Comments

57.3% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
A good system for answering this question would have been to discuss the side effects according to body system. It should be noted that some side effects of propofol are desirable for anaesthesia, but in the use of propofol as an agent for sedation are significant side effects and should therefore be discussed.
Generally, the cardiovascular and respiratory side effects were well discussed. Side effects on other body systems were less well answered.
The question specifically asked for formulations. As such side effects related to the different components of formulations gained marks.

text:
Examiner Comments

24.8% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
This repeat question was generally answered well. There was good use of classifying side effects either according to body system or the individual constituents of propofol. Propofol pharmacokinetics was not asked for. Although bacterial contamination was often mentioned, there was little understanding of how different propofol formulations are prepared to reduce this adverse effect. Extra marks were awarded for understanding the significance of certain side effects in different patient populations such as epileptics and egg allergy. Extra marks were also gained for an understanding that not all propofol formulations are prepared in the same carrier.

title: 2014A Question 2
text:
Question
Draw and explain the characteristics of a log dose-response curve that describes the major clinical effect of rocuronium. Describe how factors encountered in clinical practice may alter this curve.
Also asked in: 2013B Question 13

title: 2014A Question 2
text:
Suggested Structure
Draw and explain the curve with labelled axes and relevant intercepts. Describe each clinical factor by connecting its mechanism to the direction of the curve change.


Axes and Definition of the Measured Response


Three Phases of the Curve


ED95 and Slope


Clinical Factors Shifting or Altering the Curve

title: 2014A Question 2
text:
Examiner Comments

72.8 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
This is a two-part question. Candidates should therefore allocate adequate time for each part of the question. In the first part, most candidates were able to draw a sigmoidal “graded dose-response curve” (as opposed to a quantal dose-response curve) for rocuronium. However, many diagrams were incorrectly labelled. For instance, many candidates were unable to specify the response that should be used in the y-axis. It is important to note that the percentage of nicotinic receptors that are blocked by rocuronium cannot be measured using current clinical methods. Other important features that should be included in this curve are that (1) neuromuscular blocking effect does not occur until a significant amount of rocuronium is given because of the presence of spare receptors; (2) the points indicating ED50 and ED95; (3) the middle portion of the curve is straight and (4) there is a plateau at maximum effect. In the second part of the question, many candidates realised that a number of clinical factors (such as concomitant use of volatile agents, mixture of relaxants, hypermagnesemia, diuretics, aminoglycosides) increase the potency of rocuronium and shift the curve to the left. Whereas, use of anticonvulsants and the presence of anticholinerases decrease the potency of the drug and shift the curve to the right. A number of candidates described the pharmacology of rocuronium in detail. This is not required in the question and did not gain marks

Answers

Passing Standard
Major clinical Effect of Rocuronium:

Non depolarising muscle relaxant
Competitive antagonist at the nAChR at the NMJ
Must block ~70% of all receptor sites before clinical effect seen, no way of measuring % receptor blockade by clinical measurement.   
>70% blockade progressive reduction in twitch height.
ED95 Dose required to produce 95% reduction in twitch height in 50% of the population - for rocuronium this is 0.3mg/kg therefore ED95 Rocuronium =ED50 
Typically the induction doses used are 2-5x the ED95. 


Factors encountered in clinical practice that may alter this curve:
Factors potentiating NDMR BLOCK
Age: increased sensitising in neonates - due to immature  NMJ
Neuromuscular disorders i.e. myasthenia gravis
Drugs: inhaled anaesthetic, local anaesthetic
Electrolyte abnormalities: 
↑Mg ↑Na
↓K ↓Ca
Factors that ↑ resistance to NDMR
Anticholinesterase drug administration 
Presence of increased or extra junctional receptors: burns, prolonged immobilisation 
Motor neurone lesions 
Drugs that affect Rocuronium:
Potentate blockade:

Local Anaesthetics
Volatile agents
Aminoglycosides

↑Potency and ↑duration: failure of reversal → distress, T2RF, aspiration
↓Duration: movement when dangerous e.g. neurosurgery

Physiology

Malignant hyperthermia→ post-junctional activation

(g-cyclodextrin chelates rocuronium in plasma, increases the gradient between effect site and plasma but does not alter the dose-response curve)

Lambert-Eaton syndrome: antibody against pre-synaptic VDCC → ↓competition with ACh



Pre-synaptic drugs
↓ACh release → ↑drug: ACh ratio

↓Choline uptake: hemicholinium

↓Ion flux through nAChR

Desensitisation blockade (volatiles, barbiturates)

*All those causing ↑potency plus…*

title: 2014A Question 3
text:
Examiner Comments

32% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
To achieve a pass, candidates should have explained:

Why calibrated and accurate vaporizers are required to safely deliver different volatile anaesthetics to patients.
A definition of plenum vaporizers and brief description of their method of function, both variable bypass and injection types. Diagrams commonly contained useful information that picked up marks.
Methods for ensuring that the correct volatile anaesthetic is delivered from the correct vaporizer.
Why temperature compensation is required and how it is achieved
The role that mounting systems play in vaporizer safety.

Bonus marks were awarded for tipping and transport safety, methods of avoiding the pumping effect, MRI compatibility, electronic alarms in desflurane vaporisers and sources of leaks and how they may be avoided.
Marks were not awarded for safety features unrelated to vaporizers such as bulk gas supply, oxygen flush and end tidal gas analysis.

title: 2014A Question 3
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Plenum vaporises are a form of variable flow vaporiser where pressured gas flow is diverted into a vapour chamber. The amount of gas diverted into vaporising chamber and therefore the amount of anaesthetic vapour carried into the circuit is set by the bypass valve. It’s vital to ensure that a known, reliable concentration of vapour is delivered from the vaporiser. To achieve this there a number of key safety mechanisms:
(no need to explain how vaporiser works in detail)

Safety features of plenum vaporises include:

Agent Specific: Volatile agents have different SVP, therefore specific vaporisers are required calibrate a specific agent. To ensure the correct agent is delivered only in the correct vaporiser:

Vaporisers are only compatible with a specific volatile agent. 
Agent specific geometric design of filling inlet and anaesthetic agent container and colour coding to ensure correct agent in correct vaporiser. 
Containers and Vaporises are clearly labelled. 

Temperature: changes in temperature result in different saturated vapour pressure, ↓temperature →↓SVP and therefore ↓concentration to patient 

Container material: Vaporiser constructed of metals with high heat capacity & thermal conductivity to allow heat transfer from atmosphere to liquid and act as a heat sink
Temperature compensators: Vaporises have Bimetallic strips with different coeff of thermal expansion that alter shape \with temperature changes to change the splitting ratio

↑T°C = ↑Gas flow to bypass chamber
↓T°C = ↑Gas flow to vaporising chamber 


Flow Compensation: ↑ flow rates run risk of gas exiting the vapour chamber not being fully saturated with volatile agent

Vaporisation chamber designed with wicks/baffles to ↑ surface area of vaporisation & ensure gas leaving always fully saturated 

Pump Effect: Oscillating pressure with ventilatory cycle can alter & cause retrograde flow from the vaporiser chamber producing unpredictable variations in vapour delivered to patient

Adequate length of tubing between vaporiser and circuit
Unidirectional valve between vaporiser and circuit
Inspiratory valve prevents back pressure from patient

Pressure Compensation:

Dial in effect gives percent of atmospheric pressure. If atmospheric pressure decreases, percentage delivered by vaporises increases but final partial pressure of agent is unaffected.  

Anti-Spill Mechanism: Internal valves ensure that if vaporiser is turned upside down volatile agent cannot spill into bypass chamber



Interlocking system ensures only one vaporiser and be engaged and used at a time

title: 2014A Question 4
text:
Examiner Comments

16.8 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
In order to pass this question it was necessary to demonstrate that hypoxaemia is avoided by increasing oxygen stores and maintaining them. This mandated a discussion on the role of FRC as an oxygen store, and preoxygenation as a means of augmenting that store. Better answers demonstrated this using the alveolar gas equation. To achieve a pass, it was also necessary to provide some description on the role of positioning, and also that of apnoeic oxygenation. A discussion on the complications of all these modalities was also asked for, but frequently omitted.
Most low scoring answers included a huge amount of irrelevant information, often extending for several pages. Examples which attracted no marks included:

the role of blood transfusion
cricoid pressure (commonly discussed)
the role of video laryngoscopy
side effects of suxamethonium (commonly discussed)
the cost of sugammadex
the role of chest physiotherapy on the ward
detailed spirometery diagrams

Several candidates also asserted that preoxygenation causes diffusion hypoxia. Candidates are also reminded that rephrasing a point already made attracts no extra marks.

title: 2014A Question 4
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
A rapid sequence induction involves the rapid anaesthetic induction and paralysis of a patient for intubation and ventilation due to patient factors including increased risk of aspiration, decreased patient compliance, or patient illness. 
It’s associated with an increased risk of hypoxaemia due to (usually) no IPPV being applied to the patient prior to intubation. 
Hypoxaemia is defined as a PaO2 <60mmHg 
Method used to prevent hypoxaemia include:

Pre-oxygenation: 3-5min of normal tidal breathing on 100% O2 or 8 Vital capacity breaths with aim to denitrogenate the lungs and replace with Oxygen 

Alveolar partial pressure is derived from the Alveolar gas equation 
PAO2 = FiO2x(760-47)-(PaCO2/0.8) 
FiO2 21% = 100mmHg
FiO2 100% = 660mmHg
If FRC for normal adult is assumed 30ml/kg 2100ml then (660/760)x2100 = ~1800ml oxygen reservoir increased from 275ml at room air 
Can potentially result in absorption atelectasis  

CPAP/PEEP: Increasing ventilation in T2RF, alveolar recruitment and improving oxygenation in T1RF 

Increased pressures may result in stomachs insufflation

Apnoeic Oxygenation: Application of nasal prongs at high O2 flow rates or THRIVE to create nasopharyngeal oxygen reservoirs and facilitate apnoea mass movement and diffusion 

High flow nasal cannula can dry mucus membranes and cause epistaxis 
THRIVE tubing can affect mask seal should BVM be required 

Patient positioning increase FRC, facilities rapid intubation 

Reduced venous return → ↓ preload/reduced CO/MAP → ↓Cerebral perfusion pressure with effect of gravity






Prize

List:

Principles
Oxygen storage
Apnoeic oxygenation
Other



Principles:








Aim

Minimise time between induction and intubation



Reason

Prevent hypoxia
Prevent aspiration



Problem

Apnoea between loss of consciousness and intubation
Ongoing O2 consumption at 3-4mL/kg/min



Time to gross hypoxia

(See Nunn’s Applied Respiratory Physiology – numbers reflect ideal conditions)
Apnoeic, obstructed: <1 minute
Apnoeic, patent to room air: 1-2 minutes
Apnoeic, patent to 100% O2: several minutes
Apnoeic, patent to 100% O2, pre-oxygenated: 100 minutes







Oxygen storage:








Relevant physiology

Functional residual capacity

Volume in lungs at end of tidal expiration
Reservoir for oxygenation during apnoea

Alveolar gas equation: PAO2 = FiO2(Patm – SVPH2O) – PACO2/R

Room air → 100mmHg → 275mL O2 in FRC
100% O2 → 660mmHg → 1800mL O2 in FRC

Alveolar ventilation equation: PACO2 = VCO2 / VA x k (where PACO2 ≈ PaCO2)



Problem

Supine position → diaphragm displacement → ↓FRC to 30mL/kg
Induction → chest wall relaxation → ↓FRC to 25mL/kg



Solution
(1)Positioning:

Head up → ↓Diaphragm displacement → ↑FRC

(2)Pre-oxygenation

100% O2 3-5 mins tidal ventilation
Replace alveolar N2 with O2
↑O2 in lungs > blood, tissues, myoglobin
Room air 275mL O2, 100% O2 → 1800mL O2

(3)Hyperventilation

↓PACO2 → ↑PAO2

(4)Small amount CPAP e.g. 5cmH2O

Splint and distend alveoli
Limits ↓FRC on induction
Advantage lost at intubation



Adverse effects

Head up: may impair CNS perfusion upon induction
↑O2: absorption atelectasis, O2 toxicity in neonates
↓CO2: symptoms e.g. paraesthesia







Apnoeic oxygenation:








Relevant physiology
Alveolar gas flux during apnoea:

O2 uptake 250mL/min
CO2 output 20mL/min (PaCO2 and P­ACO2 equilibrate at 1 minute)
Net uptake by diffusion 230mL/min



Problems

Apnoea
Airway obstruction (general anaesthetic + relaxant → ↓pharyngeal dilator tone)



Solution
Prior to intubation:

Airway patency: jaw thrust, head tilt, chin lift
Face mask e.g. 10L/min of 100% O2
CPAP → splint + distend alveoli

During intubation:

High flow nasal prongs e.g. 60L/min of 100% O2



Adverse effects

Discomfort
Epistaxis







Other things that may not attract marks:


↓O2 consumption:








Problem

Anxiety → ↑SNS output
Fever



Solution

Pre-medication e.g. benzodiazepines
Human factors







Fast drugs → ↓apnoeic time: (rapid sequence by definition)








Rapid onset hypnosis

Factors ↑C1:

IV route
↑Dose
Priming dose
Rapid injection
Proximal injection
Pre-medication to reduce cardiac output
↑Unionised fraction (e.g. propofol)

Factors ↑diffusion coefficient: (e.g. propofol)

↑Lipid solubility
↓Molecular weight



Rapid onset paralysis

Similar factors
Bowman principle: ↓potency → ↑safe dose → ↑(C1-C2)
Hence fastest drugs: suxamethonium 4x ED95, rocuronium 2-4x ED95

title: 2014A Question 5
text:
Examiner Comments

37.6 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
This question has been asked before, most recently in 2013; the main points expected for a pass were addressed in the Examiners’ Report from last year.
Without a good structure, it can be difficult to answer this question and this was reflected in the marks. The better candidates described the differences in intrathoracic pressure changes between intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV) and normal ventilation then went on describe the factors that determine cardiac output: stroke volume (and its determinants) and heart rate. They explained the effects of the pressure changes during inspiration and expiration on each of these factors for both the right and left sides of the heart and the relationship between the sides.
Common mistakes included:

describing the effects on cardiac output without explaining them
mentioning preload and afterload but not explaining how these influence cardiac output
not being clear about the side of the heart being described or even mentioning that there are two sides
claiming the airway pressure gradient was reversed during inspiration with IPPV compared to spontaneous ventilation
not mentioning expiratory effects

Marks were not awarded for:

describing different modes of ventilation
a detailed description of the compensatory effects for blood pressure changes
discussion of West Zones
describing all the factors that affect pulmonary vascular resistance

title: 2014A Question 5
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Spontaneous respiration involves developing negative pleural, transpulmonary and intrathoracic pressures during inspiration.
IPPV is the intermittent application of external positive pressure to drive inspiratory flows in the ventilated patient resulting in positive intrathoracic pressures.
This results in pressure being applied to the thoracic organs and great vessels.  
Inspiration - increased intrathoracic pressure 

Increased pulmonary circulation return to the LA →  increases LV filling / preload → initial transient inc LV output
Decreased SVC/ICV Venous return reduce RV preload → Reduce LV Preload → Dec LV output
Compression of pulmonary vessels inc RV after load → Inc RV pressure  → ventricular interdependence - bulging of RV inter-ventricular septum into LV → further dec LV preload
LV Afterload is reduced as increased intrathoracic pressure decreased transmural gradient → reduced tension in LV  → inc LV performance

Expiration - decreased intrathoracic pressure 

Pulmonary vessels expand → reducing LA filling → reduced LV preload → Reduced LV output
Reduced PVR reduces RV after load → increases LV preload 
Decreased thoracic pressure increases venous return and RA filling → inc RV preload → inc LV preload and LV output returns to baseline 

Overall Effect 
IPPV has variable results depending on position on the Frank Starling curve. 
In healthy patients at the bottom of the frank staring curve IPPV → Inc Intrathoracic pressure → preload reduction → generally reduced CO
In patients with impaired CO / CCF IPPV → preload reduction → returns heart to more optimal area of curve and may inc LV performance and thus CO 
Additional Factors 
Effect of PEEP: Generally, exaggerates decreases in CO with IPPV due to reduction in RV filling pressure / preload

These changes are:

More marked in hypovolaemia
Changes are reversed with volume expansion.
Less severe with poor lung compliance
Reduced compliance greatly reduces the effect of PEEP and IPPV on the vasculature, as the change in intrapleural pressure is reduced.

title: 2014A Question 6
text:
Examiner Comments

59.2 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
The question asks candidates to outline aspects of the pharmacology of drugs used to treat asthma. Aspects to emphasize in the interpretation of this question include the drugs must be used for acute asthma, and their mechanism of action and potential adverse effects described in detail.
To obtain a good score, candidates had to mention the most important agents in more detail. These included salbutamol, adrenaline, steroids, anticholinergics, aminophyline. Additional marks were awarded for discussing other agents such as ketamine, magnesium, volatile agents, leukotriene agonists for which less detailed discussions were acceptable. Brief descriptions of the physiological implications of acute asthma also attracted marks. Mechanisms of action for each of the important agents had to include receptor subtype interaction, intermediate messengers, effect on intracytoplasmic calcium and on myosin actin interaction in smooth muscle cells lining the bronchi.
Side effects should also be mentioned in detail, with discussions regarding drugs such as steroids limited to acute side effects only.
Some additional marks were awarded for doses and routes of administration of the important agents.

Passing Standard
Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airways disease characterised by episodic airways constriction/ bronchospasm. 
Bronchospasm is a result of:

↑Bronchial smooth muscle tone 
↑ Mucus production

Acute severe asthma exacerbation results in 

↑Airways resistance and work of breathing
Gas trapping 
↑ physiological dead space

↑FiO2→↑PAO2 to compensate for reduced alveolar ventilation 

Beta 2 agonist - Salbutamol 
→ Agonist at B2 adrenergic receptor (GsPCR) →↑ cAMP →↑protein kinase A → smooth muscle relaxation 
Adverse effects: Tremor, tachycardia, hypokalaemia 
Antimuscarinic (Ipratropium Bromide) 
→ competitively inhibit M3 muscarinic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, antagonising the bronchoconstrictor action of vagal impulses
Adverse effects: ↑HR
Corticosteroids
→ Glucocorticoids are steroid hormones that bind to specific intracellular receptors and translocate into the nucleus, where they regulate gene expression in a tissue-specific manner. They are used in asthma as they cause:
Bronchodilatation by increasing bronchial smooth muscle response to circulating catecholamines
Decreased airway oedema by decreasing inflammatory responses and transudate production
Adverse Effects: insomnia, anxiety, depression, psychosis, ↑BSL if diabetic
Ketamine 
Unclear mechanism, Increases sympathetic outflow and relaxes bronchial smooth muscle
Adverse effects:
↑secretions, hallucinations, ↑SNS/MAP/HR 
Magnesium 
Physiological antagonist at L type Ca2+ channel → smooth muscle relaxation 
Adverse effects:
sedation, hypotension
Volatile anaesthetic agents
Volatile anaesthetic agents reduces bronchial smooth muscle constriction where this is pre-existing (such as asthma).
Adverse effects:
↓SVR/MAP, sedation
Leukotriene Antagonists
Selectively inhibits the cysteinyl leukotriene receptor, increased activity of which is involved in airway oedema and bronchial smooth muscle constriction

title: 2014A Question 7
text:
Examiner Comments

61.6% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
A labelled diagram would adequately show most of what was asked for in the question. This diagram especially from a lateral view schematically showing the structures or ‘layers’ from skin to the space after penetrating the ligamentum flavum was completed by most candidates. The ligamentum flavum is attached on the anterior aspects of the laminae of the vertebrae and is not a continuous layer as such
There was some confusion between the anterior superior iliac spines, the intercrestal line and the posterior superior iliac spine deciding the site of placement. The content of the epidural space which surrounds the dural sac and the cauda equina has important structures in it. Damage to any of these has significant sequelae. The vascular structures being placed generally situated in the space anterolateraly was noted in many good answers.
The technique and the description of the methodology of performing the epidural was not asked for and even if correctly outlined did not attract marks.
The mention of extra useful anatomical variations such as venous congestion during pregnancy and labour, increased fatty tissue in the obese, and origin of the arterial supply, the destination of the venous drainage, the presence of a lymphatic drainage all indicated a good understanding of the anatomy of the epidural space.

Examiner Comments

This question is lifted almost verbatim from the learning outcomes mapped to the primary examination, and is well covered in Miller and Dorsch and Dorsch. Presenting factual material from these references would easily earn a pass mark, with better marks awarded to those candidates who could integrate the scientific principles with patient safety.

title: 2014A Question 8
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Diathermy is the use of electrical current to create heat to coagulate, cut or destroy tissues during surgery.
Principles:
Uses high frequency alternating current passed between 2 electrodes.
The high frequency (300kHz and 2 MHz)is unlikely to cause arrhythmia 
Heat energy produced is proportional to electrical power dissipated 

Current density = current / area
High current density at the surgical electrode gives cutting / coagulation performance 
Low current density at the large electrode results in no tissue damage

Diathermy Types:
Unipolar:

Consists of probe containing one electrode and a large plate placed on patient containing the other electrode 

Bipolar:

Consists of a pair of electrodes in one instrument so current flows from point to point rather than through patient and is useful for electrically sensitive areas 

Surgical Uses of Diathermy 
Cutting:
Continuous low voltage high-frequency current → rapid tissue heating with AC current → tissue vaporisation. Results in cutting action with minimal collateral damage.
Coagulation:
Intermittent pulses higher voltage electrical arc from electrode or direct contact from blunt electrode → slower heating of tissue → desiccation/coagulation → increased tissue damage 
Blended:

Mix of cutting and coagulation with adjustable ration of cutting with variable pulses of coagulation 

Hazards:

Burns for incorrectly applied unipolar diathermy plate
Electrocution damage or injury to patient, staff, or equipment 
Electrical interference to pacemakers or ICDs
Smoke production, respiratory irritant and potential carcinogen

title: 2014A Question 9
text:
Examiner Comments

35.2% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
Many candidates seemed to have difficulty describing the washout or elimination phase of volatile anaesthesia and endeavoured to instead describe the kinetics of induction or uptake. Although there are many principles shared by the two phases, generally such an approach generated a muddled answer which could not score well.
To achieve a pass, the following were required:

a clear explanation of the elimination kinetics of sevoflurane with due consideration to a time course appropriate to the termination of anaesthesia after two hours.
A washout graph including appropriate axis labelling, a multi exponential decay curve, time course and half times consistent with volatile washout.
a description of the movement of sevoflurane out of the alveolus, from plasma to alveolus, from the various compartments to plasma and their respective time courses
a description of factors which underpin those kinetics, including depth and duration of anaesthesia, alveolar ventilation and fresh gas flows, compartmental blood flows and solubilities.

Additional marks were awarded for:

identifying differences in the kinetics of uptake versus elimination, describing the impact of cardiac output, an explanation of the clinical relevance of elimination kinetics

Common errors included

providing irrelevant information - the chemical structure of evoflurane , kinetic data tables without understanding, wash-in graphs, detailed discussions of Fick's law, detailed algebraic manipulations
confused graphs - nonsensical labelling - (FA/FI, FI/FA), graphing wash-in and out on the same axes, incorrect decrement rate
confusion with respect to the terms fresh gas flow and FiO2
lack of understanding of compartmental modelling and associated kinetics

Relatively low solubility oil:gas partition coefficient 43 

These properties result in a relatively rapid wash in/ washout kinetics for general anaesthesia.
Sevoflurane uptake/distribution can be modelled by the main distribution compartments, their capacity and their approximate time to reach equilibration are:

Vessel rich (Brain)- low capacity - 5min
Lean/Muscle - moderate capacity - 2.5 hours 
Fat - High Capacity - 2 days 

Washout of inhalation anaesthetic agent is dependent on establishing and maintaining a decreasing concentration gradient from compartment → blood → alveolus → circuit.  
Washout is a multi-exponential process graphed by FA/FA0 curve

↑CO → lower ΔP across alveolar membrane → slower washout

title: 2014A Question 10
text:
Examiner Comments

73.6% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
Major points expected for a pass included that tramadol was a racaemic mixture with actions as a partial mu agonist, as well as a noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Under the CNS effects, candidates should note that there is a ceiling effect to tramadol, as opposed to morphine, and hence its side effects of sedation, central respiratory depression are limited. Parasympathetic stimulation leads to bradycardia, with morphine, compared with the increased sympathetic tone seen with tramadol. Most candidates noted that both drugs cause nausea and vomiting, although tramadol has less constipation. Bonus marks were given for mention of urinary retention with morphine, histamine release effects with morphine, but not tramadol, and drug interactions between tramadol and MAOI, SSRIs. Although evidence is limited, marks were given for stating that there may be increased awareness using tramadol is part of general anaesthetic and that ondansetron may increase tramadol requirements. Tramadol has a role in neuropathic pain.
Candidates often mentioned the difference in potencies of the two drugs without emphasizing that tramadol had lower efficacy i.e. the ceiling effect of its analgesia. Few mentioned that most of the action of tramadol is due to an active metabolite, which has much higher affinity to the mu receptor than the parent compound. Some correctly mentioned that due to polymorphism of CYP2D6, the pharmacodynamic effects of tramadol could be reduced or enhanced. title: 2014A Question 12
text:
Examiner Comments

16 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
This was a relatively difficult question and marked with a great degree of latitude. This latitude did not extend so far as to give points for duplicating the question in the answer booklet. Marks were awarded, however, for dicussion of relevant alterations in the peripheral, central and autonomic nervous system.
Commonly confused issues included: Cognitive decline makes it more difficult for patients to communicate that they are in pain. It does not mean that they do not perceive pain. Most candidates did not clearly distinguish or even discuss the difference between normal ageing and the effects of disease. Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy bodies are not part of the normal ageing process. Autonomic nervous system changes were poorly understood—noradrenaline levels rise with age, but the response to beta stimulation decreases. Candidates often used afferent to mean effferent and vice versa.

title: 2014A Question 12
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Pain is defined as an unpleasant emotional or sensory perception associated with actual or potential tissue damage.
Neurological changes with ageing and their effects on pain perception can be categorised by:

Central nervous system (CNS) changes
Peripheral Nervous system (PNS) changes
Autonomic Nervous System (ANS) changes

CNS Alterations:
Ageing results in a normal process of CNS atrophy approx. 10% neuronal mass lost by 80 with progressive decline in reflex speed and cognitive processing after 80.
The above CNS alterations result in:

altered sensory and emotional perception of pain, overall ↑pain tolerance
potential inability to voice pain despite perceiving pain
potential inability to react to pain appropriately (e.g. slower withdraw from noxious stimulus)

PNS Alterations:
Ageing results in PNS atrophy of myelinated and unmyelinated axons as well as a ↓ in the number of synapses.
Afferent pain signal transduction and neurotransmitters including Substance P are decreased with ageing.
This results with decreased, slower transmission of painful stimuli to the CNS.
ANS Alterations:
Ageing results in ↑circulating noradrenaline but ↓ b1 adrenergic receptors →↓response to catecholamines and ↓ SNS tone
This results in ↓SNS/autonomic response (tachycardia and hypertension) to painful stimuli

title: 2014A Question 14
text:
Examiner Comments

59.2% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
This question required candidates to explain the differences in energy substrates and fluid balance during fasting over periods commonly encountered in clinical practice. The question specified a fast of fluids and food for a healthy adult. Some candidates did not interpret the question correctly, and attempted to discuss only fluid balance issues or food issues. Some candidates discussed fasting implications over longer periods or, more commonly, for pathological conditions such as diabetes, or even for children.
The question lends itself to answering quickly in a table format, but many answers were in prose of varying quality. Many candidates demonstrated a misunderstanding of fluid balance and energy substrates within the two timeframes.Many candidates did not appreciate the fluid loss in 6 hours amounted to approximately 1% total body water, with ADH secretion only just starting to play a role. Other systems such as the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system would not likely be significantly activated at this stage.
Commonly, answers suggested a significant fall in cardiac output, hypotension oliguria/acute renal failure and death with 24 hours of fasting. This is unlikely in a healthy adult.
Only a minority of candidates mentioned that at the start of fasting, water and food sources would still be absorbed from the GI tract, with insulin levels being elevated at this stage (pulsatile insulin secretion being high for around 2 hours post-prandially). Few candidates gave accurate accounts of the hormonal changes over the correct time frames or changes of energy substrates over the correct time frames.
Additionally there appeared to be some confusion over the terms metabolic rate, basal metabolic rate and resting metabolic rate, with many candidates suggesting basal metabolic rate would decrease over the fasting period.

Passing Standard
Foetal circulation primary anatomical and function differences:

Ductus venous 

Ductus venous shunts blood from the umbilical vein → IVC bypassing the portal circulation  

Ductus arteriosus 

Creates a flow pathway from the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta. 
High pulmonary arterial pressures due to hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction result in majority of flow bypassing lungs to systemic circulation 

Patent Foramen ovale 

Shunts blood from the right atrium to the left atrium 
Features of foetal blood flow:
Oxygen rich blood flow from the IVC directed across the right atrium and through the foramen ovale → LA → LV → Aortic Arch 
Oxygen poor blood SVC flows from the RA →  RV → DA → Descending Aorta 
Changes at birth

Placental circulation is lost / umbilical artery and venous flow cease →↑ SVR due to loss of low resistance placental circulation 
Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance from first breath - ↓RV after load - ↓RA pressures
↑ systemic pressure and ↓pulmonary circulation pressure → flow reversal through ductus arteriosus → immediate septal flap closure and sealing over hours/days under influence of prostaglandins  





Ductus arteriosus shunt reversed due to ↑mAP and ↓Pulmonary pressures →  D.O. Maintained by prostaglandin (PGE2) closure usually ~15hours after birth secondary to ↓prostaglandins reflected to ↑PaO2  





Ductus venosus remains patent for days, functionally closed after birth due to lack of umbilical vein flow

52 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question

Question
Briefly outline the acute management of malignant hyperthermia (during a relaxant general anaesthetic). Describe the important aspects of dantrolene pharmacology relevant to treating malignant hyperthermia.
Also asked in: 2007A Question 6, 2011B Question 7

title: 2014B Question 3
text:
Suggested Structure

title: 2014B Question 3
text:
Examiner Comments

28% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
There were two parts of equal importance to this question. The main points expected for acute management of malignant hyperthermia included: calling for help, early administration of dantrolene with the correct dose, active cooling, cessation of trigger agents, strategies to avoid awareness and hyperventilation with 100% oxygen. Marks were also awarded for mention of systemic supportive therapy and treatment of metabolic acidosis, arrhythmias, hyperkalaemia, myoglobinuria and coagulopathy. The relevant pharmacology of dantrolene required details of drug presentation including diluent, t1/2 and importance of such, metabolism, mechanism of action and rate of onset. Additional marks were given for recognising effect on mortality, specificity for skeletal muscle, side effects and important interactions. Common mistakes included vague statements, repetition of information in the two sections and incorrect information. No marks were awarded for definitions of malignant hyperthermia, description of genetic basis, details of excitation-contraction coupling or post acute management/follow-up testing. Statements regarding pathophysiology only attracted marks if a clear link was made to management or drug action.

title: 2014B Question 3
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Malignant Hyperthermia (MH):
MH is a rare autosomal dominant genetic condition. Prevalence – approx. 1:15,000 (range 1:10,000 ~ 220,000)
Triggers include depolarising muscle relaxants (Suxamethonium) and volatile anaesthetic agents.
MH involves the mutation of the ryanodine receptor that results in excessive calcium to leave the sarcoplasmic reticulum → continual muscle contraction.
Clinical features include: 

↑ CO2
↑Temperature 
increased lactate 
Muscle spasm
Acidosis and hyperkalaemia 
CVS instability 

Acute Management intraoperative:

Call for help / MH kit
Cease volatile agent and change to TIVA, washout with 100% O2 at maximum flows
Add charcoal filters to circuit - change soda lime is easy
Give dantrolene 2.5mg/kg  
Manage hyperkalaemia and acidosis 
Invasive and non-invasive cooling as appropriate 

Dantrolene: 
Physiochemical:
Orange powder, vials of 20mg Dantrolene and 3g Mannitol 
Reconstitute in sterile water - can be difficult to dissolve 
Venous irritant 
Dosing: 
2.5mg/kg - repeat 10 minutely 
PK
Absorption: IV only in MH
Distribution: VD 0.6 L/kg; 90% protein bound
Metabolism: hepatic metabolism; major metabolite is 5-hydroxydantrolene, which is
active
Elimination: renally excreted, half-life 9 hours
PD:
MOA: 
Dantrolene is a ryanodine (RYR1) receptor antagonist, which prevents release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, uncoupling the process of excitation-contraction.
Skeletal muscle relaxation
Side effects are rare and include GIT side effects and




Prize

List:

Summary
Immediate Mx
Dantrolene pharmacology



Summary:








Definition

Rare, life-threatening hypermetabolic reaction to volatile anaesthetics or suxamethonium



Aetiology

Autosomal dominant mutation RYR1 gene encoding the skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor (RR) and ion channel
1 in 200,000



Pathophysiology

Continuous, excessive Ca2+ release
Continuous skeletal muscle contraction
↑↑VO2, ↑↑VCO2
↑HR, ↑etCO2, ↑temp



Complications

Rhabdomyolysis
Acidosis
Arrhythmia
Death (80% mortality if untreated)







Immediate treatment:








Basics

Call for help, need many hands
Abandon surgery
Stop the offending agent(s) ASAP

Cease volatile, FGF >10L/min to flush circuit, ↑FiO2 to 100%
No more suxamethonium

Start IV sedation e.g. propofol 30mL/h



ABC

A: insert ETT
B: IPPV, note ↑↑MV required
C: ensure BP within safe limits, insert arterial line
D: sedate e.g.propofol 200mg/h



Dantrolene ASAP

Bolus dose: 2.5mg/kg rapidly ± repeat; may require >10mg/kg
Infusion for up to 24h: 1mg/kg/h



Cool to 37C

Remove clothing and blankets
Cold IV saline
Cold bladder or intraperitoneal irrigation



Treat complications

e.g. hyperkalemia



Take to ICU

Observation ~24 hours
+/- dantrolene infusion







Dantrolene pharmacology:








Physicochemical

Glass vial, orange powder
20mg dantrolene, 3mg mannitol (solubiliser), NaOH
Add to 60mL H2O
Needs mixing +++ (poorly water soluble)
± thrombophlebitis
± necrosis if extravasated



Pharmacokinetic

IV or oral
Low VD 0.6L/kg
90% plasma protein bound
Hepatic metabolism Phase 1; active metabolite 5-OH-dantrolene
Renal excretion of metabolites
t1/2β 9 hours



Pharmacodynamic

Competitive antagonist at the skeletal muscle RR → ↓Ca2+ release → post-junctional relaxation
Effects: skeletal muscle relaxation, resp paralysis
No effect on cardiac or CNS ryanodine receptor
Side effects rare:

↑LFTs
APO from IV fluid +++

title: 2014B Question 4

Examiner Comments

5 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
To gain a pass mark candidates needed to describe the components, functions and features of an active scavenging system. This could be done by dividing the scavenging system into components:

collecting assembly (shroud) – input from APL and ventilator
transfer system – specific tubing features and occlusive problems
receiving system or scavenging interface – flow control, reservoir, valve functions, system volume

Additional marks were awarded for diagrams, stating why scavenging is important, circumstances where scavenging is not effective, and potential problems with the system. Marks were awarded for explaining the difference between an open and closed active system were rewarded.
Marks were not awarded for comments on passive systems, greenhouse gas effects or descriptions of soda lime. Descriptions of an operating theatre air-circulation system was not considered relevant. title: 2014B Question 5
text:
Examiner Comments

50 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
Better answers were based upon an anatomical approach. More complete answers had a definition of pain, location and stimuli of peripheral receptors, pain fibres (A delta and C fibres), cord pathways (including dorsal horn lamina, neo and paleospinothalamic tracts), central perception, descending pathways, and the modulation by drugs at each of these points. More detail gained extra marks. Diagrams, although useful, often resulted in a lack of detail, for example labelling C and A delta fibres without providing additional information, or repeating what was already written down. When discussing modulation by drugs, a mechanism of action was expected, not just the class or name of the drug. The use of the word ‘etc’ did not attract marks.
crumbs: Q5: Pain pathways and drug modulation

title: 2014B Question 5
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Pain is an unpleasant sensory or emotional experience associated with potential or actual tissue damage. 
Pain Pathways can be described in terms of:
Transduction

Transduction occurs from noxious stimuli stimulating peripheral nociceptors (free nerve endings), stimuli may take the form of mechanical, thermal, electrical or chemical.
Transduction is the process of noxious stimuli → electrical impulse  

Transmission
Pain impulses are conducted by two main types of pain fibres Aδ (A delta) or C fibres to the dorsal horn where second order neutrons transmit impulses to brainstem and thalamus by the spinothalamic and spinoparabrachial tracts.

Aδ fibres are small myelinated fibres that conduct sharp pain rapidly @ 40m.s, they mediate the initial pain reflex to acute pain. 
Synapse in the laminae I in the dorsal horn and substance P is the neurotransmitter at the NK1 receptor 





C Fibres very small unmyelinated fibres the conduct dull pain slowly at 2m.s
Synapse at laminae II of the dorsal horn  Substance P is the neurotransmitter at the NK1 receptor

Perception

Third order neurones  from the thalamus project to the higher centres including the somatosensory cortex and limbic system
Results in the sensory and emotional perception of pain 

Modulation 
Pain perception may be modulated either inhibited or sensitised via :

depending pathways i.e. the gate theory of pain 
via ascending pathways i.e. central sensitisation / wind up 

Drug Modulation: 
Drugs form an important role in management of pain through modulation at different sites/levels, some drugs act at multiple points to modulate pain. 
Transduction:

Drugs may modulate the perception of pain from peripheral nociceptors.
NSAIDS inhibit COX →↓prostaglandins  →↓ sensitisation of nociceptors 

Transmission:

Local anaesthetics inhibit sodium channels → disruption of pain impulse transmission
Opioids activate MOP receptors upregulating inhibitory resending pathway → inhibition of nervy impulse at spinal level 
TCA, SSRI and SNRI  → increase NA and 5HT in spinal cord + brainstem inhibit pain signal transmission, also act to modulate pain perception and modulation 
A2 adrenergic agonists (e.g. clonidine and dexmedetomidine presynaptic and postsynaptic inhibitory effects at dorsal horn and brainstem
Tramadol SSRI and MOP acts to decrease transmission and perception and modulation  

Perception and Modulation

Ketamine NMDA antagonist reduces windup and central sensitisation





Prize

List:

Nociceptive receptor
Primary afferent
Secondary afferent and tracts
Tertiary afferent and above
Descending modulation



Nociceptive receptor:








Physiology

Free nerve ending on 1° afferent in periphery
Activated by mechanical, thermal, chemical insults
Sensitised by inflammation
Ionotropic and metabotropic



Pharmacology

Local anaesthetic (LA): inhibits VDNaC
NSAID: inhibits prostaglandin-induced receptor sensitisation and activation







Primary afferent (nociceptor):








Physiology

From periphery → dorsal horn, with cell body in dorsal root ganglion
Ascent or descent 1-2 levels via Lissauer’s tract

Aδ fibre:

Releases glutamate
Synapse at superficial layers.
Sharp, fast, well localized (i.e. somatic pain)

C fibre:

Releases glutamate, substance P
Synapse at deeper layers.
Dull, slow, poorly localized (i.e. visceral pain)

Silent nociceptor:
Conveys pain only when sensitized


Pharmacology
Pre-synaptic inhibition:

Neuraxial LA: VdNaC at dorsal root ganglion, spinal nerve root
Opioid
Noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake inihbitors
Gabapentinoids: antagonists at synaptic VdCC α2δ subunit
Cannabinoids: at own receptor

Other:

Paracetamol: inhibits bradykinin-sensitive nociceptors
Regional LA (nerve, plexus): inhibits axonal VDNaC







Secondary afferent and tracts:








Physiology: cell

Nociceptive-specific: superficial layers, variable threshold
Wide dynamic range: deeper layers, high threshold, only when sensitized
Note also interneurons: excitatory and inhibitory
Note inhibitory afferents: e.g. Aβ conveying light touch



Physiology: tracts

Decussation in anterior commissure
Ascent in spinothalamic tracts

Neo-STT: to thalamus (VPL nucleus)
Paleo-/archi-STT: to brainstem




Pharmacology

Post-synaptic inhibition:

NMDA antagonist: ketamine, N2O, Xe, Mg2+, tramadol, methadone








Tertiary afferents and above








Physiology:

VPL thalamus → primary somatosensory cortex (localisation)
Brainstem → medial thalamus, hypothalamus, amygdala (affective, autonomic)



Pharmacology

NMDA antagonist (as above) → thalamocortical dissociation
Paracetamol: COX-3 inhibition
General anaesthetics: inhibit brainstem ARAS → no perception







Descending modulation:








Physiology

Pathway: PAG or RVM → dorsal horn via Lissauer’s tract
Mediators: noradrenaline → serotonin
Effect: inhibit 1° afferent (pre-synaptic) and 2° afferent (post-synaptic)



Pharmacology

Opioids: ↓activity of OFF cell → ↓Inhibition of ON cell
Noradrenaline reuptake inhibition: ketamine, tramadol, tapentadol, NRI
Serotonin reuptake inhibition: tramadol, SSRI
Dorsal horn α2 agonism: clonidine, dexmedetomidine
