title: 2014B Question 6
text:
Examiner Comments

51% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
The wording of this question describes a situation that is a life-threatening medical emergency. An appreciation of this was lacking in many answers. The potential complications are cardiovascular and CNS toxicity. The correct CC/CNS ratio for bupivacaine with an explanation of the significance of this ratio in the situation described assisted candidates. A number of candidates miscalculated the dose of bupivacaine being administered and others confused maximum safe dosing, toxic doses and what occurs when a near maximum dose of bupivacaine is administered intravenously. The question asked for the mechanism by which bupivacaine caused toxicity as well as a description of CNS and the CVS signs and symptoms. Some answers incorrectly described the mechanism of channel blockade. Better answers included a calculation of an expected plasma level and related this to toxic plasma levels. General information about local anaesthetics, the treatment of local anaesthetic toxicity, local anaesthetic allergy and tissue toxicity were not relevant.

title: 2014B Question 6
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Bupivacaine is an amide local anaesthetic agent. 
Safe tissue dosage is recommended as 2mg/kg → 60kg person 120mg.
20ml of 0.5% bupivacaine = 100mg dose. However this has been delivered to blood volume → >20mcg/ml concentration this is a life-threatening dose. 
CNS toxicity usually seem around 2mcg/ml plasma volume 
The ratio of dose required to produce cardiovascular collapse (CC) to  that required to produce seizures (CNS) is a measurement of cardiac toxicity of and LA agent.
Bupivacaine has a  CC:CNS ration of 2, much lower than other LA agents (lignocaine 7) → faster progression from CNS symptoms → Cardiovascular collapse. 
Mechanism of action:
Unionised Bupivacaine diffuses across the nerve axon phospholipid membrane 
In the axon → ionised and blocks Na channel in inactivated state 
→ nerve inhibits depolarisation
Major causes of toxicity:
CVS:
Na channel blockers including bupivacaine are Class I antiarrhythmic agents and act at Phase 0 of the cardiac myocyte depolarisation → inhibits and decreases rate of depolarisation → bradycardia, AV conduction delay  → ↓HR/asystole and ↓mAP → cardiovascular collapse 
CNS
Initial excitatory effects

Inhibition of inhibitory interneurons
Peri-oral tingling, tinnitus, vertigo, slurred speech, inattention, twitching, seizures

Then inhibitory effects

Inhibition of excitatory interneurons and others
Coma, apnoea

title: 2014B Question 7
text:
Examiner Comments

29 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
In order to pass the question, candidates were required to provide an accurate definition of sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV). A 2x2 contingency table was often helpful for explaining definitions, especially when the terms true positive, true negative, false positive and false negative were represented correctly within the table.
Extra marks could be gained for recognizing that difficult intubation is a relatively uncommon event, with potentially serious consequences if unpredicted. Recognising that a low “disease” prevalence reduced the PPV and increased the NPV was rewarded, as was a realisation that sensitivity and specificity are unaffected by the “disease” prevalence. Marks were also gained for mentioning that a large, and representative, sample population is required when determining the test characteristics initially and for stating that the test may not give the same results in different population groups. Common sources of error were: incorrect definitions of specificity; confusing sensitivity and specificity with positive and negative predictive value; stating that disease prevalence affected sensitivity and specificity and the use of the acronym “SPecificity rules IN, SeNsitivity rules OUT (SPIN SNOUT)” which in virtually every instance resulted in incorrect definitions, possibly due to its inherently misleading nature.

Question
Outline the important pharmacological considerations when stopping warfarin and commencing prophylactic (low dose) low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) in the peri-operative period.
Also asked in: 2007B Question 2

title: 2014B Question 8
text:
Suggested Structure

title: 2014B Question 8
text:
Examiner Comments

60% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
The main points expected from candidates to pass this question are a discussion on the pharmacokinetics and the pharmacodynamics of both warfarin and low molecular weight heparin (LMWH). Drug interactions and pathophysiological factors (e.g. liver or renal dysfunction) that may potentiate the actions of both drugs were included in good answers. Pre-operatively, warfarin is ceased for 5 days in elective cases and the checking of INR prior to surgery provides a measure of coagulation status of the patient.
Prophylactic LWMH is commenced 2-3 days after warfarin is ceased and it should be ceased 12 hours prior to surgery and neuraxial blockade. The rationale of this practice and the details of how bridging therapy is managed were discussed in good answers. A balance of excessive bleeding versus the risk of thromboembolic events is the guiding factor in most clinical cases. Extra marks are given to answers that recognize urgency of surgery sometimes necessitates the reversal of warfarin with various available pharmacological agents. The details of commencement of post-operative anticoagulation were frequent omissions.
This question specifically asked for an outline of bridging therapy with prophylactic low dose LMWH upon cessation of warfarin in the peri-operative period. Lengthy discussions on the merits of not using bridging therapy, the benefits of using unfractionated heparin instead of LMWH and the requirements of therapeutic anticoagulation in some patients are not within the scope of this question.

What lower limit of SpO2 would you accept in an ASA1 young male under general anaesthesia? Explain your reasons for choosing this value.

title: 2014B Question 9
text:
Suggested Structure
State the lower limit you would accept, then explain it by connecting saturation to oxygen tension, content and delivery in the specified patient.

Relationship to SaO2, PaO2 and Oxygen Content


Oxygen Delivery, Demand and Compensation


Chosen Limit: Duration, Reserve and Measurement Uncertainty
crumbs: Q9: Lower acceptable SpO2 under anaesthesia

title: 2014B Question 9
text:
Examiner Comments

30 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
To construct a good answer, this question required the candidate to integrate a number of syllabus areas.
Candidates should begin with defining SpO2, and establishing a normal range. The relationships between SpO2, SaO2, paO2, oxygen content and oxygen delivery should be explained, as well as the factors that affect these relationships. All proposed lower limits of acceptable SpO2 gained marks, so long as the reasoning was valid.
The SpO2 that correlated with hypoxaemia was often proposed. Assorted definitions of hypoxaemia were offered. The deleterious effects of borderline hypoxaemia were often not mentioned, or overstated. Expected acute compensatory mechanisms were rarely mentioned. Duration of hypoxaemia should be considered when setting a lower acceptable limit.
Terms such as “physiologic reserve” and “acute compromise” should not be used without adequate explanation.
crumbs: Q9: Lower acceptable SpO2 under anaesthesia

title: 2014B Question 9
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
A partial pressure gradient is required to drive oxygen transport from alveoli to cells/mitochondria for cellular respiration. 
Hypoxaemia is typically defined as a PaO2 <60mmHg, while brief periods of hyperaemia are generally well tolerated by healthy people, prolonged hyperaemia will lead to metabolic derangement cellular dysfunction and cell death.   

SpO2 is a measurement of the percentage of haemoglobin saturated by oxygen using pulse oximetry
SaO2 is % saturation measured by blood gas analysis and usually closely correlates with SpO2.   

SpO2 is a useful measurement as a surrogate of PaO2 using the oxygen-haemoglobin disassociation curve.
Common reference points are:
PaO2 90mmHg → SpO2 99%
PaO2 60mmHg → SpO2 90%
PaO2 27mmHg → SpO2 50%
Oxygen delivery is dependent on multiple factors as described in the flux equation. 
DO2 = CO (SpO2xHbx1.34) + (0.003xPaO2) 
→ ↓ SPO2 may be compensated by ↑ CO 
The considerations being cardiac output, SpO2 and haemoglobin concentration.
VO2 is often reduced under anaesthesia in healthy patients undergoing elective surgery.
Therefore, the lower limit of SpO2 I would accept in an ASA1 patient under general anaesthesia would be 94% for the following reasons. 

Provides adequate PaO2 (approx. 75mmHg) for normal cellular respiration, avoids hyperoxia while allowing for increased shunt under Anaesthesia. 
Allows safety for measurement error of pulse oximetry, patient or equipment airway/ventilation complications 
Provides a buffer to the steep part of the disassociation curve  for any decreases in PaO2
Lower SpO2 should provoke consideration of causes of desaturation in a an ASA1 young male without pre-existing cardio/respiratory disease

title: 2014B Question 10
text:
Suggested Structure
Explain how renal blood flow is regulated by connecting perfusion pressure and vascular resistance to the control mechanisms. Organise the physiological effects of angiotensin II by system.


Renal Blood Flow: Definition, Normal Values and Determinants


Myogenic Autoregulation and Tubuloglomerular Feedback


Neural, Local and Hormonal Control


Angiotensin II: Cardiovascular, CNS, Renal and Autonomic Effects
crumbs: Q10: Renal blood flow and angiotensin II

title: 2014B Question 10
text:
Examiner Comments

57% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
Better answers were written with a reasonable structure that included:

A definition of renal blood flow, with normal values
Flow = renal perfusion pressure / renal vascular resistance.
The anatomy of renal blood supply (only a brief description was necessary) and recognition that the vascular tone of the afferent and efferent arterioles is the main determinant of renal vascular resistance.
Describing autoregulation between a range of mean arterial pressures (A wide range of values was accepted here).
An explanation of myogenic autoregulation. This was often overlooked or not discussed in much detail.
Notes about tubuloglomerular feedback, including the structure and function of the juxtaglomerular complex, and the activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone cascade.
The role of the sympathetic nervous system.

Additional points were awarded for extra detail about release and effects of local and circulating hormones (such as ANP/noradrenaline/adrenaline/adenosine/NO/prostaglandins) on afferent and efferent arteriole tone. Common errors included: confusing glomerular filtration rate and renal blood flow, vague and imprecise statements about effects of different hormones, omitting detail and listing bullet points without explanation.
Effects of angiotensin II: A list of these was sufficient for a pass mark – in particular the cardiovascular, CNS, renal and autonomic effects. Further marks were awarded for an increased level of detail. For example, most candidates were able to write that angiotensin II was a potent vasoconstrictor. More marks were awarded if this was followed with a description that angiotensin acted on peripheral arteries and veins, leading to an increase in SVR and MAP. The renal effects were reasonably well described, but few candidates explained that angiotensin II has a greater effect on the efferent arteriole than the afferent arteriole. Credit was given if candidates could explain that the net effect of an increased level of angiotensin II is to increase water/salt retention and increase the effective circulating volume.

title: 2014B Question 10
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Normal value for renal blood flow is 1l/min (500ml each kidney) → approx. 20% of CO 
Determinants of renal blood flow:
Renal blood flow follows ohms hydraulic law:
Renal blood flow = renal perfusion pressure / renal vascular resistance.
Renal bolos flow this there determined by cardiac output/MAP and subject to regulation through adjustment of renal vascular resistance.
Resistance to venous return determined by Hagen Poiseuille equation

R most important determinant as its to power of ‘4’
Renal blood flow is regulated through 3 mechanisms:
Autoregulation

Myogenic Autoregulation 

Myogenic regulation refers to the intrinsic ability for the afferent arteriole to constrict in response to increased stretch maintaining proportional ↑vascular resistance for ↑pressure → constant flow 

Tubuloglomerular feedback 

Tubuloglomerular feedback is mechanism of the macula densa influencing afferent and efferent arteriole dilation/constriction based on concentration of solutes reaching the macula densa at the junction ascending loop of hen lie/DCT and the junction of the afferent/efferent arteriole entering the glomerular capsule. 
↑ filtrate flow →↓ reabsorption of Na → high concentration at the macula densa → release of adenosine → constriction of the afferent arteriole  
↓ filtrate flow →↑ reabsorption of Na → low concentration at the macula densa → release of NO and renin  → dilation of the afferent arteriole  
Neuronal Regulation

Kidneys are supplied by sympathetic nervous system

→ NA → a1 receptors → afferent arteriolar constriction →↓ Renal Blood flow 
→ NA → B1 receptors in juxtaglomerular cells → release of renin 
Hormonal Control 

Renin released from Juxtaglomerular cells 

→ Catalyses the production of angiotensin I from circulating angiotensinogen
→ angiotensin I + ACE → angiotensin II
Angiotensin II has the following effects (on renal blood flow) 

→ release of ADH from posterior pituitary 

Effects of Angiotensin II
Angiotensin II increases blood pressure via a number of mechanisms:

Simulates aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex, increasing sodium and water retention
Vasoconstriction of efferent greater than the afferent arterioles
Results in slight decrease in GFR at a lower perfusion pressure, but increases filtration fraction.


NB: Different sources quote different changes (increase or decrease) in GFR The final effect may vary depending on the contribution of other autoregulatory processes.


Reduces Kf through constriction of glomerular mesangial cells
Increased SNS activity and central and peripheral vasoconstriction
Increases thirst via hypothalamic stimulation
Stimulates ADH release, reducing renal water excretion
Stimulates release of angiotensinogen

CVS effects

Potent vasoconstrictor + venoconstriction →↓venous capacitance + ↑SVR →↑preload + ↑afterload →↑MAP

CNS effects

Acts at OVLT, SFO and other periventricular organs to stimulate thirst →↑fluid intake →↑circulating volume
Stimulates autonomic nervous system!↑SNS tone

Renal effects

Vasoconstriction efferent > afferent arterioles!↓RBF and defends precipitous fall of GFR during hypovolaemia overall leads to ↑circulating volume
Acts on adrenal cortex (zona glomerulosa) ↑aldosterone secretion!↑Na and water retention by kidneys (DCT/CCD mechanisms) and ↑K excretion

title: 2014B Question 11
text:
Question
Describe the cardiovascular changes that occur with morbid obesity.
Also asked in: 2016B Question 5, 2018A Question 2

title: 2014B Question 11
text:
Suggested Structure
Describe the cardiovascular changes systematically, connecting each altered variable to its mechanism. Distinguish changes in obesity itself from associated disease.


Cardiac Output, Heart Rate and Stroke Volume


Blood Volume and Preload


Vascular Resistance and Afterload


Ventricular Structure, Function and Reserve


Hormonal Influences and ECG Changes

title: 2014B Question 11
text:
Examiner Comments

3 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
This question required an understanding of the cardiovascular changes in obesity per se as opposed to those associated with the co-morbid conditions of hypertension, diabetes and coronary artery disease. Candidates who used a systemic approach, such as describing the changes in cardiac output, heart rate, stroke volume, systemic vascular resistance, afterload, preload and contractility, did better. There were many misconceptions about the cardiovascular physiology in the uncomplicated obese patient especially regarding systemic vascular resistance/afterload and heart rate. Adipose tissue does not compress the arteries causing hypertension. Obese patients do not have increased resistance due to longer blood vessels. Otherwise all tall people would be hypertensive as well. In fact, fat vascular beds are added in parallel so systemic vascular resistance is normal or even reduced. An explanation of the mechanism behind the altered physiological variable was expected. Obese patients do not have a resting tachycardia to maintain cardiac output. Many mentioned increased blood volume but failed to equate this to increased preload and stroke volume. The mechanism behind left ventricular hypertrophy in obesity was misunderstood. Non-hypertensive obese patients still have left ventricular hypertrophy. Extra points were awarded to ECG changes, the cardiovascular responses to exercise and to the understanding of the hormonal changes that underpin the majority of cardiovascular changes seen in the obese patient.

title: 2014B Question 12
text:
Examiner Comments

31 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
Good answers to this question contained definitions and descriptions of the Bohr and Haldane effects and also a summary of transplacental gas exchange, indicating why these two effects are important in this special organ bed. A diagram with accurate values for gas tensions and saturations was an effective way of summarizing gas exchange in the placenta.
The double Bohr and double Haldane effects were usually described at length- the same number of marks could be earned with a single well constructed sentence covering the same principles, thus saving time.
In any question about physiology it is important to describe the physiological effect but also the mechanisms behind it; the physiology at a molecular level of haemoglobin involved in the Haldane effect was often described in this question but the characteristics of haemoglobin specific to the Bohr effect were not.

title: 2014B Question 12
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
The placenta connects the foetus to the uterine wall and is responsible for exchange of oxygen, nutrients and waste products between the foetal and maternal circulation.
At the placenta O2 and CO2 diffuse passively down their concentration gradients. 
gas diffusion is governed as elsewhere by Fick’s law:
Q= AkΔP/T
A = diffusion area
k= solubility / (square of MW)
ΔP= concentration gradient 
T= diffusion membrane thickness 
Placenta is much less efficient in gas exchange then lungs due to:

↓Surface area 14m2 compared with 70m2 in lungs
↑diffusion membrane thickness 3.5micrometer compared to 0.5micrometer in lungs

Normal values that establish the diffusion concentration gradient are:





Maternal
Foetal Umbilical Artery 
Foetal Umbilical Vein 




PO2
~80mmHg
~19mmHg
~28mmHg


PCO2
~40mmHg
~55mmHg
~40mmHg




Bohr Effect
The Bohr effect describes how an increase in PaCO2/H+ shifts the oxygen haemoglobin curve to the right and ↓Hb affinity for oxygen → ↑ offloading of oxygen.
Double Bohr Effect
In placental exchange CO2 from the foetus diffuses across the placenta increasing offloading of maternal oxygen while on the foetal side the relative  ↓ PCO2 → ↑ HbF affinity for O2
The effect of this is to help drive oxygen diffusion across from maternal → foetus.
 Haldane Effect 
The haldane effect describes how as maternal PaO2 levels decrease, haemoglobin’s capacity for CO2 carriage increases. 
Double Haldane Effect
The double haldane effect describes the additional process in the foetus where ↑ HbFO2  levels → ↓HbF Capacity for CO2 
The effect of this is to drive CO2 exchange from foetal → maternal 
The overall combination of these effects is the increase in separation of the maternal and foetal disassociation curves whereby the maternal Hb is right shifted (promoting dissociation) and the Foetal Hb is left shifted (promoting oxygen binding)

title: 2014B Question 14
text:
Examiner Comments

67 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
It was difficult to pass this questions without addressing both parts; specifically, effects and potential problems. Most successful candidates identified 20% mannitol as an osmotic diuretic. An outline of its effects was ideally presented under headings that included effects on plasma osmolarity and the renal tubules. Better responses identified the phasic nature of mannitol’s effects. An outline of cardiovascular effects via volume load and subsequent plasma expansion was also rewarded. However, lengthy and intricate discussions of Starling’s forces, baroceptor reflexes, and the cellular mechanisms of natriuretic peptides and anti-diuretic hormone were usually at the expense of scoring elsewhere. More detailed physiological discussions often become self-contradictory. Despite identifying mannitol as an osmotic diuretic, some argued that it works at the renal tubule via an osmoreceptor response that upregulates antiduretic hormone sectretion in the pituitary. Potential problems associated with use were best identified separately, either as a discrete section or contrasted against the effects. These problems could be outlined under headings that included: circulatory overload, dehydration and hypovolaemia, electrolyte disturbances, and rebound effects.

title: 2014B Question 15
text:
Examiner Comments

46 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
A definition of sleep was expected, as well as an explanation of the stages of sleep: non-REM (stages 1 to 4), and REM. Candidates were frequently confused about these points – for example, stating that REM is stage 4, or that stage 1 is awake. The EEG changes occurring in each stage were required, however EEG changes were often quoted with little or no explanation (e.g. “delta waves” without defining this as high amplitude, low frequency EEG). Marks were awarded for explaining the relative times spent in each stage, how this changes as sleep progresses, and changes through the lifespan.
Significant marks were available for explaining the respiratory changes in sleep. This was poorly addressed in the majority of answers. There is a reduction in tidal volume (not respiratory rate), with only very slight changes in PaO2 and PaCO2. The reduction in tidal volume is greatest during REM sleep. Although pharyngeal tone is decreased, with snoring common, it is not normal to develop sleep apnoea, become hypoxic, or have Cheyne-Stokes breathing when asleep. The respiratory changes are covered in detail in Nunn’s Applied Respiratory Physiology.
Other points able to gain marks included the effects of sleep on: cardiovascular, temperature, skeletal muscle, GIT, endocrine/metabolic, and renal systems. Also the reasons for sleep, and effects of sleep deprivation. Very few candidates mentioned the CNS circuitry which produces sleep, or the neurotransmitters involved.

title: 2015A Question 1

Examiner Comments

28.1% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
To gain a pass mark candidates were required to provide a definition of a circle system, list the components of the circuit and their functions, and draw an accurate diagram showing the placement of the components. Candidates that explained the reasons for placing components in specific positions were awarded further marks. Additional marks were awarded for explanations of clinical relevance.
Common errors included inaccurate circuit diagrams, describing the system as non re-breathing and use of imprecise statements. Discussions on the chemical reactions of soda lime, vaporiser function, anti-hypoxic devices, oxygen supply lines and different ventilator modes and functions did not gain marks.

title: 2015A Question 1
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Circle breathing system = closed (or semi-closed) circuit used to delivery oxygen and anaesthetic gases, while eliminating carbon dioxide, which involves recirculation of patient’s respiratory gases 

Components of Circle System 

Fresh gas inflow – provides O2 to match O2 consumption; provides gas flow to wash out expired gas 
Inspiratory and expiratory tubing (usu. corrugated) – conducts gas flow 
Inspiratory and expiratory unidirectional valves – ensures unidirectional flow
and prevents mixing of inspiratory and expiratory gases minimise rebreathing 
Wye connector – separates inspiratory and expiratory limbs 
Adjustable pressure limiting (APL) valve – prevents high pressures within the circuit; prevents patient subjected to high pressures 
Reservoir bag – stores gas between respiratory cycles, provides tactile feedback of respiration, enables circuit to be manually pressurised 
Carbon dioxide absorber – removes expired CO2 from circuit 
Other (non-essential) components of anaesthetic circle include

ventilator 
flow meters 
vaporiser 
out of circuit sampling line + gas analyser 
heat and moisture exchanging filter 


Advantages and Disadvantages 
Advantages 

constant inspired concentrations 
conserves heat and humidity 
allows low fresh gas flow rates 
rebreathing of anaesthetic gases reduces cost and pollution

Disadvantages 

complex and prone to malfunction/leak
increase dead space

title: 2015A Question 2
text:
Examiner Comments

29.2% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
This question was first asked in the 1956 (then FARACS) primary examination, and has been frequently asked over the last 60 years. It asked about the role of carbon dioxide in ventilation.
Candidates were expected to point out that as a product of metabolism, carbon dioxide (CO2) provides a key link in the control loop that matches ventilation with metabolic rate to maintain a stable PaCO2 level.
It was expected that the elements of this control loop and its negative feedback nature were described. In particular, the central and peripheral chemoreceptors with their relative contributions, the central controlling by the respiratory centre in the brain stem, the ultimate effect on minute ventilation via the respiratory muscles and the consequent changes to PaCO2.
Describing factors that influence the gain and threshold of this system such as PaO2 (both increased and decreased), anaesthesia, sleep, and blood pH were rewarded. Discussing the blunted nature of the ventilation response at low and high PaCO2 also gained marks.
Drawing the graph of ventilation versus PaCO2 gained marks only if drawn correctly.
Common mistakes included:

confusing the location of the central chemoreceptors
reversing the rapidity of response between central and peripheral chemoreceptors
writing an equation showing PaCO2 inversely proportional to ventilation then drawing a graph that demonstrated a direct relationship between ventilation and PaCO2 but not explaining that these related to different parts of the control loop.
stating that CO2 could not cross the blood-brain barrier but hydrogen ions could

Marks were not awarded for:

Describing how CO2 is carried in the blood
Explaining how CO2 influences the oxygen haemoglobin dissociation curve.

title: 2015A Question 2
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Carbon Dioxide is a product of cellular respiration Produced at a rate of approx. 200ml/min in a healthy adult and is usually tightly controlled around a PaCO2 of 40mmHg. 
The quantity of CO2 produced for O2 consumed is the respiratory quotient (RQ) and changes as per diet.

For a healthy adult enacting a combined diet including animal products the RQ is usually 0.8.
Carbohydrate Diets the RQ is 1.0
Lipid Diets the RQ is 0.7

Ventilation is controlled by a system of sensors, regulators and effectors which operative by a negative feedback loop whereby increasing levels of CO2 stimulate increase minute ventilation by increasing tidal volume and respiratory rate.
Sensors:
Peripheral chemo receptors in the Carotid Body and Aortic Body detect increases in CO2 and decreases in pH (Carotid Body only). This is carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve respectively to the respiratory centre in the medulla. 
Peripheral receptor contribution to stimulation ventilation is a fast response however considered weaker (20% of total) then the central receptor.
Central Chemoreceptors are sensitive to decreases in pH secondary to increased diffusion of CO2 through the BBB (which is impermeable to H+) and accumulation of CO2 in the CSF. This CO2 is enzymatically catalysed by carbonic anhydride to for H2CO3 that disassociated into H+ and HCO3-, resulting in ↓pH.
Central Controller:
The respiratory centre receives afferent supply from chemoreceptors increases RR by increasing stimulation from the dorsal respiratory group → TV and RR. 
Effectors
Phrenic Nerve → Diaphragm
Vagus and Intercostal Nerves → respiratory muscles including the external and internal intercostal muscles and the accessory muscles including sternocleidomastoid.
In healthy spontaneously breathing subjects, there is a progressive and rapid increase in MV (approx. 3L) for each 1mmHg increase in PaCO2 over 40mmHg. ↓pH has a synergistically response where CO2 with increase MV at a lower set point (<40mmHg). 

Influences on the ventilator response to CO2 include:

PaO2 - both increased and decreased
Anaesthesia and opiates decreases sensitivity to ↑PaCO2 and ↓PaO2
Sleep

title: 2015A Question 3
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
The liver is crucially placed at the interface between the gut and the circulation to the rest of the body. It separates the portal and systemic circulation.
Protective Roles:
Immunity

Liver protects the body against microbes
Kupffer cells are phagocytes that are situated in the hepatic sinusoids that absorb and degrade bacteria and endotoxins as part of the innate immune system. Antigens can be used to stimulated the adaptive immune system 
Synthesis of complement and acute phase reactants 

Detoxification: liver performs major role in detoxification and metabolism of drugs and processing for elimination through phase I and Phase 2 reactions 
Regulatory Roles 

Glucose regulation: The liver regulates blood glucose in tight range absorbing blood glucose through GLUT 4 transporters activated by insulin to reduce blood glucose levels, its able to store glucose in inactive form as glycogen and synthesis fatty acids. The liver is able increase plasma glucose by glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
Metabolism of metabolic acids such as ketones and lactic acid  
Protein and lipid metabolism 
Regulating production of albumin to control plasma oncotic pressure
Production of bile in regulating fat and fat-soluble vitamin absorption
Bilirubin metabolism





Prize

List:

Protective: immunity and detox
Regulatory: macronutrient supply, blood volume, oncotic pressure, coagulation status



Protective:








Innate immunity

Filter portal blood
Kupffer cells: phagocytosis, cytokine secretion (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α)
Synthesises complement (opsonization, lysis, chemotaxis)
Synthesises acute phase reactants (CRP activates complement, Ferritin, α1 antitrypsin)



Adaptive immunity

Kupffer cells: present antigens to TH cells
(Kupffer cells are macrophages lining the sinusoids)



Detoxification

Affects toxins and drugs
Oral route via portal blood = first pass metabolism. Barrier between gut and rest of body.
Other routes via hepatic arterial blood
Phase 1 reactions: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis. By CYP450. Usually inactivates.
Phase 2 reactions: glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, methylation. Usually solubilizes
Large, lipid soluble metabolite → bile, faeces
Small, water soluble metabolite → urine







Regulatory:








Macronutrient concentrations
Carbohydrates:

Islet β-cell = glucostat, liver = major effector
Constitutive GLUT-2 = free glucose movement
Direction of glucose flow controlled by hexokinase activity, not portal blood [glucose]
Insulin → ↑uptake, ↑trapping as G6P (↑hexokinase, glycogenesis, DNL, glycolysis)
Glucagon, cortisol, SNS → ↑release (↓hexokinase, ↑glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis)

Proteins:

Amino acid synthesis (↑insulin:glucagon) and breakdown (↓insulin:glucagon)
Transamination (ALT, AST)
Uptake and release into circulation as required

title: 2015A Question 4
text:
Examiner Comments

48.9% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
This question consists of two parts: Part 1: To score marks in part 1 there had to be some possibility that the patient could survive the administered doses. Part 2: Three areas should be addressed. i) The sodium channel effects on the central nervous system. ii) The sodium channel effects on the heart. iii) The effects caused by noradrenaline/serotonin re-uptake inhibition. Current data suggest there are less serious events if cocaine is given with adrenaline than without it, however individual patients may have idiosyncratic reactions.
Commonly confused issues included: A 1% solution is 10mg/ml not 1mg/ml or 0.1mg/ml. If your dose calculation is giving you a ridiculous value, you should consider the possibility you have made a mistake. The limited data suggest that CNS toxicity is additive. Cardiovascular toxicity is more complex. CNS toxicity is not confined to lignocaine, as cocaine is a local anaesthetic in its own right. The amount of adrenaline injected with local anaesthetic rarely causes serious problems. It is not safer to increase the dose of cocaine in order to give less lignocaine and adrenaline. Nasal septal necrosis is not commonly seen after a single dose of cocaine used in ENT surgery.

title: 2015A Question 5
text:
Examiner Comments

15.7% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
This question was previously asked in the first sitting 2013 when a higher percentage of candidates passed this question. The most common error made was to provide a table detailing often a considerable number of pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties and then failing to relate this to the question. This was particularly the case with the pharmacokinetic properties of each drug.
To pass this question candidates needed to recognize that these drugs complement each other in terms of providing balanced anaesthesia and that they have synergistic actions with regards to their CNS depressant actions. Synergism allows a reduced dose of each drug to be administered reducing the adverse effects associated with these drugs when given in isolation at a higher dose. Detail regarding these concepts as well as specific examples of how they facilitate decreased adverse effects was expected. Better candidates used correctly labelled isobolograms to enhance their answer and noted the cost savings as well as provided examples of the benefits of the combination in surgical subspecialty groups, e.g. obstetrics- fentanyl reducing the dose of sevoflurane which can cause uterine atony.
Several candidates provided detail regarding situations where the drug combination was not helpful and this did not attract merit. Several candidates incorrectly asserted that the combination of drugs decreased the rate of PONV of either agent alone. A considerable number of candidates falsely stated that fentanyl did not possess any sedative or anaesthetic properties.

title: 2015A Question 6
text:
Examiner Comments

52.8% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
Answers that achieved a good mark contained information about high pressure baroreceptors and their locations, how mechanoreceptor firing pattern changes with arterial blood pressure, neural pathways to the CNS, a summary of how central integration occurs modulating sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow and the effect on heart rate and systemic vascular resistance. Describing the response to both an increase and then a decrease in arterial blood pressure did not earn more marks- a note that the physiological responses follow the same pathways but are opposite in these situations demonstrates understanding without consuming valuable time.
Also required for a complete answer was information about low pressure baroreceptors on the venous side of the circulation which tend to have a longer term effect on blood pressure by affecting hormones controlling intravascular volume via the kidney. High pressure baroreceptors have a more immediate effect to counter acute changes such as those resulting from postural changes.
Many candidates described the effect of atrial naturetic peptide but then did not cover the renin-angiotensin/aldosterone system or vasopressin. Detailed description of the effects of these hormones and their synthetic pathways was not required.
Extra credit was given for describing how baroreceptor reflex arcs could be tested with a Valsalva manouevre, the role baroreceptors play in the Bainbridge and Bezold Jarish reflexes and the effect and reversibility of chronic hypertension.

Examiner Comments

38.8% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
This question lent itself to breakdown into manageable parts: The effects of sevoflurane on each muscle type, the mechanisms relevant to each of the tissue effects, and the clinical significance of those effects. To score well, candidates needed to emphasise relaxant skeletal muscle effects and atypical effects characterised chiefly by MH. An appreciation of the types of smooth muscle - vascular and non vascular, in addition to the clinically unique relevance of specialised circulations such as the cerebral vasculature was a prerequisite for a high score. It was necessary to describe the effect on cardiac muscle specifically rather than on the circulation in general as this tended to result in a confused answer that failed to distinguish vascular smooth muscle and cardiac muscle effects. Too many candidates consumed time rewriting the question or providing lengthy details of sevoflurane’s pharmaceutic and kinetic properties for which no credit could be obtained. Examiner Comments

83.1% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
A pass mark required at least 5 classes of drugs to be listed with their accompanying mechanisms of action. It was necessary for candidates to realize that the oral route and drugs only given that way would not be available, as was the urgency of treatment rather than including slower onset agents.
Marks were awarded to those utilizing and specifically mentioning drugs to treat inadequate depth of anaesthesia and analgesia as well as the specific anti-hypertensive agents. In particular it was expected that intravenous and volatile anaesthetics would be included in the list, along with opioids. Specific antihypertensive such as selective beta blockers, nitrovasodilators, alpha 2 agonists and alpha 1 antagonists were required.
Structured answers where drugs were grouped according to actions generally facilitated the awarding of marks, although in some instances this led to missed opportunities for individual drug mechanisms of action. Extra marks were awarded for including magnesium, labetalol, calcium channel blockers and centrally acting agents.
Many answers included extraneous material which was not awarded marks by the marking guide such as details about how blood pressure is generated or the end results of untreated hypertension. There was also some confusion about the actual mechanism of action of the vasodilators GTN and SNP.

title: 2015A Question 9
text:

title: 2015A Question 9
text:
Examiner Comments

43.3% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
To achieve a pass, candidates were required to define FRC, and explain the majority of following points in terms of a reduced FRC – oxygen store, lung compliance, airway resistance, work of breathing, pulmonary vascular resistance, FRC falling below closing capacity, low V/Q with increased physiological shunt and hypoxaemia. Appropriately labelled diagrams which were relevant to the points being described, attracted higher marks.
When considering the consequences of decreasing FRC by 1 litre, it is essential to consider its initial volume. Normally, a 70 kg adult has an FRC of 3 L when standing, and this decreases to 2.2 L when supine (a decrease of 800 mL, usually tolerated very well). See Nunn 7 th ed, Fig 3.10, p.38. However, a decrease by 1 L from an already low FRC (e.g. a supine patient, or with pathology such as obesity), can have significant adverse consequences. Only two candidates considered these points in their answer.
Candidates should note that listing the normal functions of FRC, followed by a description of a reduced FRC wasted time and resulted in the same information being written out twice with no extra marks. Vague terms like “V/Q mismatch” or “compromised breathing” gained no marks. Many candidates confused dead space with shunt. Others were confused about gas trapping (this is not the cause of atelectasis as FRC falls below closing capacity). Many candidates wrote at length about the role of FRC in preoxygenation, at the expense of gaining marks with other, equally important points. Treatment strategies aimed at increasing FRC were not relevant to the question.

title: 2015A Question 9
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Functional residual capacity is the residual volume + expiratory reserve volume or otherwise described as being the lung volume remaining at the end of tidal expiration. It is the point at which the balance between the forces of chest wall outwards recoil and lung elastic recoil and surface tension intersect.
FRC is usually 30ml/kg or approx. 2100ml in a healthy adult. 
Causes of reduced FRC include decreased respiratory compliance, decreased muscle tone due to anaesthesia, obesity, pregnancy, and patient positioning such as supine. 
Reducing FRC by 1 (approx. 30-50%) litre has multiple physiological consequences:

Decreased lung compliance, at FRC the lung should be on the steep portion of the compliance curve. Decreasing FRC would likely decrease the lung compliance resulting in greater transpulmonary pressures being required to inflate the lungs. 
Reduced alveolar diameter with reduced FRC would result in increased alveolar collapse/atelectasis and subsequent reduced gas diffusion/exchange surface area.
Closing Capacity (CC) is the lung volume at which the small airways collapse. In a healthy 44 year old adult closing capacity exceeds FRC supine while it exceeds FRC in an erect 66 year old. Decreasing FRC results is CC exceeding FRC in normal ventilation resulting in increased atelectasis and reduced gas exchange → increased risk of hypoxaemia 
Pulmonary Vascular resistance Is increased at volumes above or below FRC. Reducing FRC results in increased pressure on extra alveolar vessels and will result in increased PVR
Due to decreased radial tension on airways at decreased FRC the smaller diameter of airways would result in increased airway resistance
Decreased Reservoir Pre oxygenation in anaesthesia, in preoxygenation the FRC is denitrogenofied and produces an oxygen reservoir for metabolism during apnoea. Reducing FRC would therefore reduce the date apnoea time





Prize

Intro: definition and significance
Determinants of FRC
Effects of 1L reduction in FRC



Intro: functional residual capacity (FRC)

Point at which lung inward recoil = chest wall outward recoil
Sum of residual volume + expiratory reserve volume



Normal

Upright: 40mL/kg (~2,800mL)
Supine: 30mL/kg (~2,100mL)



Significance of 1L decrease in FRC

Large reduction (30-50%), close to residual volume
From upright FRC: well tolerated
From supine FRC: poorly tolerated, especially if obese, pregnant







Determinants of FRC:








Absolute lung size

Age: adult FRC > child
Sex: male FRC > female
Height: taller FRC > shorter



Alveolar patency

Atelectasis → ↓FRC:

Obstructive: e.g. mucus plugging
Compressive: e.g. pregnant → supine compression by gravid uterus
Absorptive: e.g. 100% FiO2 (especially if narrowed airway)

Positive airway pressure → ↑FRC

PEEP → prevent collapse, distend alveoli
Recruitment manoeuvres → re-open collapsed alveoli




Lung inward recoil

Intrinsic elasticity: e.g. emphysema → ↑FRC (e.g. smoking, age ↑1% per year)
Surfactant: e.g. premature neonate → ↑surface tension → ↓FRC



Chest wall outward recoil

Intrinsic elasticity: e.g. neonate (cartilaginous ribs) → ↓FRC
Distortion of chest wall: e.g. pregnancy, kyphoscoliosis → ↓FRC
Diaphragm and intercostal tone: ↓FRC 15% under GA (paralysed or not)

Effects of 1L reduction in FRC:








(1)↓O2 Reservoir

↓O2 for gas exchange when apnoeic (and between breaths)
↑Speed of desaturation
At supine FRC 1.1L:
Room air: reservoir 145mL, desaturation <1 minute
Pre-oxygenated: reservoir 955mL, desaturation <4 minutes



(2)Impaired gas exchange

When closing capacity > lung volume:
↓Distending transpulmonary pressure
↑Airway closure and alveolar collapse
↑Physiological shunt
↓PaO2




(3)↓Compliance

↓Static compliance: due to ↓Lung volume → ↓alveolar radius

LaPlace’s law: tension = pressure x radius / 4

↓Dynamic compliance: due to re-opening of collapsed alveoli

Starling resistor effect

Overall ↓compliance → ↑work of breathing




(4)↑Airway resistance

Laminar flow: R = (8 x length x viscosity) / (π x radius4)
Turbulent flow: (P1-P2) ∝ (length x density) / (radius5)
↓Lung volume → ↓airway radius → ↑resistance
Radius major factor, since power 4 or 5




(5)↑Pulmonary vascular resistance

Low volume: compress extra-alveolar vessel
High volume: compress alveolar vessels


With 1L reduction in FRC:

New equilibrium at reduced FRC
But ↓FRC → ↓all vessel radii → ↑resistance

title: 2015A Question 10
text:
Examiner Comments

21.3% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
This question required candidates to explain the physiological reasons which contribute to a commonly encountered clinical problem and as such required quantification of a normal and reduced urine output, with an explanation of the glomerular, tubular and collecting duct systems and neuro-humoral controls involved in the normal production of urine. A subsequent logical discussion of how pre-renal, renal and post renal perturbations of these could result in low urinary output resulted in higher marks.
Most candidates readily identified decreased perfusion through hypotension and/or myocardial depression as contributory. However adequate descriptions of renal autoregulation were less frequent. Many candidates concentrated on all the possible causes of intra-operative hypotension, rather than describe how glomerular filtration, tubuloglomerular feedback and other mechanisms may lead to oliguria.
Comments regarding pathological conditions did not gain marks, since the question specifically stated the patient was otherwise well.
Many answers gave significant weighting to surgical misadventure (renal , ureteric , bladder and urethral trauma) which, although possible, is more uncommon than the normal physiological response to stress.

title: 2015A Question 10
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard

Normal urinary production is approx.: 0.5-1ml/kg/hr. 
Oliguria is the production of less than 0.5ml/kg/hr.

Urine formation and concentration is a product of filtrate production and reabsorption.
Intraoperative oliguria may result in an otherwise healthy person through:

Reduction in filtrate formation 
Increased Filtrate reabsorption mechanisms

Mechanism of Filtrate Formation:
Filtrate production is a result of GFR and Renal Blood Flow 
GFR normally 125ml/min 
GFR = NFP x Kf
Kf = filtration coefficient = capillary permeability and membrane surface area, designated Kf
NFP = balance of starling forces across the glomerular membrane
= Capillary Hydrostatic Pressure - Capsular hydrostatic pressure - Capillary Oncotic Pressure 
(Protein not normally filtered) 
Renal blood flow = Renal perfusion pressure (mAP-CVP) / Renal vascular resistance 

Renal Blood flow is usually 1l/min / 20% of cardiac output 
Renal blood flow is auto regulated between mAP 65-165mmHg 

Regulation of RBF and GFR 
Generally auto-regulated between mAP 65-165mmHg

Myogenic Mechanism: stretch receptors in the afferent arteriole respond to changes in perfusion pressure by dilating / constricting to maintain a relatively constant blood flow. 
Tubuloglomerular feedback: ↓Filtrate flow →↓Na at the Macula Densa →↓adenosine release → dilation of afferent arteriole + ↑Renin release → RAAS pathway
Neuronal Control:  NA release  → 

stimulation of B1 receptors at the juxtaglomerular apparatus → renin release → RAAS Pathway 
stimulation of a1 receptors → arteriole constriction →↓ GFR

Hormonal  Control:  RAAS pathway:

Renin converts Angiotensinogen → Angiotensin I, converted by ACE) → Angiotensin II which has the following effects:

↑ADH release → V1 agonism → potent vasoconstriction; V2 Agonism →↑ water reabsorption →↑ mAP 
↑ Aldosterone release →↑Na/H2O reabsorption →↑intravascular volume 
 Efferent and afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction 
↑SNS activity →Vascular constriction →↓RBF
↓filtration coefficient (Kf) 



Factors decreasing filtration:
↓ Renal blood flow due to: 

↓mAP: Anaesthetic agents and regional anaesthetic techniques →↓SVR +/- ↓CO
↑CVP: Invasive ventilation and PEEP →↓Renal perfusion pressure + ↓preload 
↑Renal vascular resistance: due to activation of above auto regulation mechanisms, neuronal and hormonal control mechanisms

Reabsorption Of Filtrate
Filtrate reabsorption is primarily performed automatically, with urine volume and concentration adjusted through changes in reabsorption in the DCT and collecting system → formation of dilute or concentrated urine is based on aldosterone and ADH 

ADH released from the posterior pituitary → V2 receptors in the \ in the collecting duct → aquaporin molecule insertion → increased filtrate reabsorption / formation of concentrated urine

→↑ Aldosterone → increased Na/H2O reabsorption from DCT 
Factors increasing Reabsorption: 
Preoperative fasting/↑ fluid losses →↑ADH →  ↓urine volume ↑Urine osmolality
Activation of auto-regulative RAAS pathway →↑Aldosterone →↑Sodium and H2O Reabsorption → decreased urine production

title: 2015A Question 12
text:
Examiner Comments

24.7 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
The February/March 2010 examination report provides a detailed report for this exam. The question is in two parts and asks the candidate to describe and explain each stage of the time course to onset of anaesthesia. Marks were awarded for graphs depicting the plasma and effect site concentrations vs time together with typical levels at which loss of consciousness would occur. Explanations using pharmacokinetic compartment modelling together with discussion about equilibration rate constants between compartments attracted marks. Discussion about determinants of movement between compartments using Fick’s Law of Diffusion also attracted marks. Marks were awarded for an explanation of the effect site concept. A description of the role of the effect site equilibration rate constant (keo) and equilibration half-life (t1/2keo) in the delay in onset was expected. Extra marks were also awarded for discussion about how different intravenous anaesthetic drugs differ in their pharmacokinetic characteristics that lead to differences in onset time. Changes in physiological or pathological states that affected pharmacokinetics attracted bonus marks.
Common omissions were descriptions of each stage in the time course. Explanations about the effect site concept and equilibration rate constants were commonly mistaken. General discussions about a drug’s pharmacokinetic profile not related to its onset time did not attract marks.

title: 2015A Question 13
text:
Examiner Comments

34.8 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
Most candidates were able to highlight drug interactions at the level of neuromuscular junction. Specifically, candidates were expected to describe the effects of volatile anesthetics, magnesium, calcium channel antagonists and aminoglycosides on the release and response of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. A good answer needed to include the mechanism, direction and magnitude of effects. In addition, the dose of rocuronium given and the duration since last dose administered would have major effect on the recovery and reversal of rocuronium-induced neuromuscular block. Candidates should also mention the effects of anticholinesterase and use of γ-cyclodextrin.
Majority of candidates provided details on the general pharmacology of rocuronium. This is unnecessary and inevitably reduced the time that was available to score points that are essential to this question.

title: 2015A Question 13
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Rocuronium is an intermediate-acting aminosteroid non-depolarising muscle relaxant
Mechanism: competitive antagonist of nAChR at NMJ
Post-synaptic nAChR antagonism → muscle relaxation
Intubating dose 0.6mg/kg produces paralysis within 60-120s for ~30mins
>70% receptor occupation required for paralysis
Recovery of neuromuscular function depends on:
a. Rocuronium at NMJ
b. PK factors 
b. PD factors
Concentration of Rocuronium at NMJ

Increasing dose of rocuronium →↑Rocuronium at NMJ →↑time for diffusion back into plasma →↑duration of block 
Time since administration →↓time since administration →↑ plasma/NMJ Concentration →↑time till recovery 

PK Factors
Distribution
Singe Bolus dose - ↑ rate of recovery as redistributed 
Repeat dosing - ↓ rate of recovery due to accumulation 
Metabolism: 
< 5% hepatic metabolism → ↓rate of recovery with: Hepatic dysfunction; hypothermia (↓enzymatic function)
Elimination:
70% hepatic/biliary clearance → longer duration in hepatic dysfunction 
30% renal dysfunction → longer duration in renal dysfunction 
PD Factors
Volatile agents 
→ Potentiate Blockade 
↑Skeletal muscle blood flow and ↓muscle tone / motor activity from CNS/spinal cord
Magnesium
↑Magnesium → Potentiate Blockade
↑Mg2+ → antagonize Ca2+ at L-Ca2+ channel → reduced ACh release 
Calcium Channel Antagonist 
→ Potentiate Blockade
↓Ca2+ influx  →↓ACh release 
Aminoglycosides: 
→ Potentiate Blockade 
Aminoglycosides →↓Ca2+ influx  →↓ACh release
Physiological States:
Elderly → ↓ muscle mass ↓Vd → longer duration 
Pregnancy → ↑ GFR, ↑Vd ↑hepatic enzymatic function → ↑ rate of recovery 
NMJ Disease:
Myasthenia Gravis → ↓nAChR → ↑ sensitive to Roc
Reversal Agents:

Anticholinesterases such as neostigmine →↑ ACh at NJM → decrease time to recovery 
Gamma cyclodextrin (sugammadex)  → forms complex with rocuronium in plasma → concentration gradient to remove roc from NMJ
reversal action/effectiveness and speed of reversal dependant on depth of blockade when administered (amount of Roc at NMJ) and dose of reversal given

title: 2015A Question 14
text:
Examiner Comments

43.8 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
Better organised answers tended to recognize that the question was in two parts and therefore explained the physiological determinants of venous return first. Candidates used these principles to discuss how pharmacological agents, positioning, surgical interventions, e.g. pnuemoperitoneum, and positive pressure ventilation altered the volume of blood returning to the right atrium per unit time. Many candidates did not recognize that stroke volume per se is not a determinant of venous return and that cardiac output although linked and interdependent is also not a direct determinant of venous return.
A pictorial representation of the venous return vs. right atrial pressure curve was useful to demonstrate changes in venous resistance and mean systemic filling pressure and, when drawn and labeled correctly, this gained extra marks.
Although presented differently, all the reading list physiology texts provide good summaries of this area of physiology, and marks were awarded for any of the reading text interpretations.
crumbs: Q14: Venous Return and General Anaesthesia

title: 2015A Question 14
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
The venous circulation returns a blood to the right atrium via the SVC and IVC
The venous system is a capacitance low pressure system and by continuance principle returns the same volume as cardiac output. 
Venous return = (Mean Systolic Filling Pressure - Right Atrial Pressure) / Resistance to Venous Return 
Venous return peripherally is driven my muscle pumps action with valves to ensure forward flow 
Determinants of VR and Effects of GA 
Factors that ↑MSFP

↑blood volume
↑venous Tone
Posture/Gravity i.e. legs up / head down position 

Effect of Anaesthesia 

↓MSFP 

blood loss from surgery/dehydration from fasting 
Vasodilation due to anaesthetic agents 

↑MSFP 

Operative position (Trendelenburg/lithotomy)


Factors that ↑RAP 

↑Intrathoracic pressure 
↑Alveolar Pressure → ↑PAP  

Effect of Anaesthesia 

PPV/PEEP → ↑Intrathoracic pressure → ↑RAP
↓ contractility 

Factors that ↑RVR 

Venous diameter 

Effect of Anaesthesia 

Pneumoperitoneum 
Venodilation 

Other Factors:

↓venous return due to lack of muscle pump action in anaesthesia 
Lack of negative intrathoracic pressure System





Prize

List:

Venous return physiology: curve, equation, components
Factors affecting MSFP
Factors affecting RAP
Factors affecting RVR



Venous return physiology:








Curve



Equation

Venous return = (mean systemic filling pressure – right atrial pressure) / resistance to venous return


Hence factors increasing venous return: ↑MSFP, ↓RAP, ↓RVR
Anaesthesia generally decreases venous return due to ↓MSFP



Definitions

Mean systemic filling pressure (MSFP):

Pressure in the systemic circulation when heart is arrested and equilibrium reached
Dependent upon a) systemic blood volume b) capacitance of the vasculature.

Right atrial pressure (RAP):

Pressure in right atrium at end of diastole, at end expiration

Resistance to venous return (RVR):

1/3 due to arterial resistance
2/3 to venous resistance


(Note in vivo, venoconstriction increases MSFP more than it increases RVR)


Summary

Anaesthetic agents dilate venous capacitance vessels
Large amount of blood shifts from stressed volume to unstressed volume
Reduced venous return
Severely exacerbated by hypovolaemia







Factors affecting MSFP:








Circulating volume

Blood loss → ↓volume → ↓MSFP



Venous tone

↓SNS output → venodilatation → ↓MSFP (e.g. GA, neuraxial)



Posture

Trendelenburg → ↓venous pooling → ↑MSFP
Reverse Trendelenburg → opposite



Skeletal muscle pump

Walking → soleus/gastrocnemius activity → compression of venous plexuses
Immobilisation, paralysis → absence of pump



Venous valves

Venodilators → +/- valve incompetence (e.g. GA, neuraxial)







Factors affecting RAP:








Cardiac function

RV contraction → RA elongation → ↓RAP (not a direct determinant)
GA → ↓contractility → ↑RAP



Intrathoracic pressure

Spont vent → ↓intrathoracic pressure in inspiration → ↓RAP
Positive pressure ventilation → absence of respiratory pump and ↑RAP







Factors affecting RVR:








Arterial diameter

Vasodilators → ↓RVR (e.g. GA, neuraxial)
Pneumoperitoneum → ↑SVR → ↑RVR



Venous diameter

Venodilators → ↓RVR (e.g. GA, neuraxial)
Pneumoperitoneum → IVC compression → ↑RVR

Question
Compare and contrast the effects of general and neuraxial anaesthesia on thermoregulation.
crumbs: Q15: General and Neuraxial Anaesthesia and Thermoregulation

title: 2015A Question 15
text:
Suggested Structure
Compare and contrast the modes in parallel columns. Link sensory, central and effector changes to thresholds and heat redistribution, then compare the magnitude and phases of temperature change using labelled graphs.





Feature
General Anaesthesia
Neuraxial Anaesthesia




Thermal Sensors and Afferents




Central Integration and Interthreshold Range




Behavioural Responses




Autonomic Heat Conservation and Production




Heat Loss and Temperature Phases
crumbs: Q15: General and Neuraxial Anaesthesia and Thermoregulation

title: 2015A Question 15
text:
Examiner Comments

41 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
Anaesthesia impairs thermoregulation in a dose dependent manner, leading to hypothermia in the perioperative period, and marks were awarded for details of how these modes impair thermoregulation.
The hypothalamus is the central integrator for thermoregulation. Interthreshold range is the core temperature range that does not induce automomic thermoregulatory reflexes to maintain temperature. Points were given for its value and how general anaesthesia affects the range.
Radiation is the main source of heat loss. General anaesthesia impairs peripheral vasoconstriction, allowing redistribution of core heat to the periphery, which accounts for the relatively large initial loss of core temperature in the first hour of anaesthesia.
Marks were awarded for comparison of the degree of impairment of the two modes on thermoregulation, for e.g. shivering is abolished under general anaesthesia, but only below the level of the block in neuroaxial anaesthesia. Graphs of the triphasic response garner additional marks, as did the graph of the widening of the intertheshold range with GA.
Many candidates did not comment on the magnitude of the changes with different modes of anaesthesia. Many candidates were not aware that neuroaxial anaesthesia has a central effect, and of the absence of a plateau phase in combined anaesthesia.
crumbs: Q15: General and Neuraxial Anaesthesia and Thermoregulation

title: 2015A Question 15
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Thermoregulation is a homeostatic mechanism that aims to maintain a constant core body temperature

Interthreshold range is the range of core temperatures over which no autonomic thermoregulatory responses occur. Approx. 37C +/- 0.2C in non-anaesthetised state
General Anaesthesia effects on Thermoregulation:
GA causes 1-3C core body temperature over 3 phases
Phase 1 

Occurs over first 30min-1 hour  
↓1.5C initial rapid phase of loss due peripheral vasodilation and subsequent heat loss from redistribution from core to peripheries
Inter-threshold range is increased from 0.4°C to 4°C

Phase 2

Further core temperature drop over ~2hours of ~1°C 
Heat loss is a result of heat loss exceeding heat production as non-shivering thermogenesis is only response available to paralysed anaesthetised patient

Phase 3 Plateau

Thermoregulatory responses are activated and vasoconstriction constrains heat to core 
Increased metabolic heat production
Heat loss may still exceed heat production 

Neuraxial Anaesthesia effects on Thermoregulation:

Hypothermia is generally less extreme as thermoregulation is only affected in areas covered by blockade → larger the blockade →↑effect on thermoregulation and temperature 
Plateau phase does not occur  as vasoconstrictive responses are inhibited by the blockade





Prize

List:

Intro
Overall effect of anaesthesia
Sensor
Controller
Behavioural effectors
Autonomic effectors: heat conservation/gain
Autonomic effectors: heat loss



Intro:








Thermo-regulation

Tight control of temp ~37°C
Heat loss = heat gain except over short period
Maintains function of enzymes and ion channels, metabolic rate, blood Viscosity
System = sensors + integrator + effectors
Dose-dependent impairment of thermoregulation
Hypothermia (<36°C) common peri-operatively



Modes of heat loss

Radiation 40%
Convection 30%
Evaporation 15%
Respiration 10%
Conduction 5%







Overall effect of anaesthesia:








Graph



Phase 1

Distribution ∝ (Tcore- Tperiphery) at onset of anaesthesia



Phase 2

Heat loss > heat production



Phase 3

Vasoconstriction constrains heat to the core
Peripheral temp continues to fall
Note heat loss rate may still exceed heat production rate



Recovery phase

Core temp normalizes over 2-5 hours post-op







Sensors:








Physiology

Ambient temp: skin

Warm receptors: Ruffini endings via C fibres (active >30°C)
Cold receptors: Krause bulbs via Aδ fibres (active <25°C)

Core temp: spinal cord, deep thorax and abdomen
Afferents via spinothalamic tracts



General anaesthesia

↓All afferents



Neuraxial aneasthesia

↓Afferents below block level (loss of heat afferents may be the cause of shivering)







Integrator and controller = hypothalamus:








Physiology

Receives afferents
Regulates set point (single target temperature)
Regulates inter-threshold range (range of core temp over which no thermoregulatory response occurs; normally 36.8-37°C)
Controls behavioural and autonomic effectors



General anaesthesia

↑Inter-threshold range from 36.8-37.0 (0.2°C) to 34.3 – 38.3 (4°C)



Neuraxial anaesthesia

↑Inter-threshold range ∝ number of segments blocked
Max reduction in lower threshold 0.6°C
Loss of tonic thermal input from spinal cord receptor)
Preserved cold perception, can ask for help







Behavioural effectors:








Heat conservation

Go to warm place → ↓temp gradient
Put on clothes → insulation → ↓convection
Curl up → ↓surface area



Heat loss

Rest (↓heat production)
Hide from sun (↓radiation gain)
Take off clothes (↑convection)
Pant (↑evaporation) – unimportant in man
Lie on a cold surface (↑conduction)



General anaesthesia

Ablated responses



Neuraxial anaesthesia

Impulses preserved
Ability to respond impaired







Autonomic effectors: heat preservation:








Vasoconstriction

↓Skin blood flow and volume → ↓skin temp → ↓gradient → ↓radiation, convection, conduction



Shivering

↑Metabolic rate 2-3x → ↑heat production



Brown fat metabolism

↑MR 2-3x → ↑heat production
Only significant in neonates



Calorigenic hormones

Effect of catecholamines etc. on skeletal muscle, liver



General anaesthesia

All impaired
Rapid distribution of heat from core to periphery by vasodilation



Neuraxial anaesthesia

Responses ablated below block level, even when threshold reached







Effectors: heat loss








Vasodilation

↑Skin blood flow and volume → ↑skin temp → ↑gradient → ↑radiation, conduction, convection



Sweating

Evaporation → loss of latent heat



General anaesthesia

Both impaired



Neuraxial anaesthesia

Both impaired below block level

title: 2015B Question 1
text:
Examiner Comments

61.5 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
This question asked candidates to discuss the pharmacology of ketamine in acute pain management. It's a good idea to circle or underline the concepts 'ketamine' and 'acute pain management' on the paper, and to ask yourself as you go along if every point you write is discussing the use of ketamine in acute pain management. I would estimate about half of the total words written overall discussed the use of ketamine in anaesthesia which gained no marks. The exam is a stressful environment and you should work out strategies beforehand that will ensure you answer the question.
Many candidates appropriately used the familiar trope of pharmaceutics, pharmacokinetics etc to address the first part of the question. When discussing pharmaceutics you will do better making comments on potentially neurotoxic preservatives and differing analgesic activities of the isomers in a racemic mixture, than you will making comments on the solution being clear and colourless, which again is not relevant to its use in acute pain management. Basic memorised pharmacokinetic data is well worth writing, a better answer discusses the relevance of first pass metabolism and an active metabolite to oral administration. No marks are gained for generic comments such as defining the IV route as having 100% bioavailability. Analgesic doses needed to be considered when discussing pharmacodynamics. There were marks allocated for a description of ketamine's analgesic mechanism of action.

title: 2015B Question 1
text:
Answers


  
    Hide Answers
    Passing Standard
    Prize
    Both Answers
  

No model answers available.



Passing Standard
Ketamine is a dissociative anaesthetic agent with analgesic properties  
Pharmaceutics:
Suitable for use is wide range of environments and applications due to stability and lack of special storage / preparation requirements

Stable in solution
No toxic additives (benzethonium chloride: theoretical risk of neurotoxicity)
Low risk of bacterial growth (suitable for slow infusion in single syringe)
Not painful on injection (suitable for peripheral IV)

2 optical isomers (S (+) and R (-))

S (+) - Better analgesia, rapid metabolism, less intense emergence side effects 

Pharmacokinetics:
Administration for analgesia:

Able to be given PO, IM, IV 
High first pass metabolism, Bioavailability 17% orally, 30% S/L
Rapid onset in IV form useful as rescue analgesia and for procedural analgesia in ED/prehospital settings 
IV infusion avoids peaks and troughs, useful analgesia adjuvant, titratable 
IM/Sublingual useful for situations where IV use problematic including, ward dressings, combat and transport settings

Distribution:

Vd 4/kg, pKa 7.5 60% unionised, PB 25%
low protein binding 
high lipid solubility 
T1/2a 10-15min, t1/2b 2-4 hours 

Metabolism:

Hepatic primarily by CYP3A4
Active metabolite norketamine (30% as active)

Elimination in urine, Cl: 15ml/kg/min
Pharmacodynamics
Analgesic Effects
MOA

Non-competitive antagonist at NMDA and glutamate receptors 
Muscarinic AChR Antagonist 
Opioid agonist 

Action
Effective for Acute and chronic pain 

Post-synaptic inhibition at dorsal horn → ↓Pain signal transmission
Short term: ↓excitability, ↓wind-up
Long term: ↓synaptic reinforcement, ↓long-term potentiation

Adverse effects:
CNS: Hallucinations, delirium, SNS Stimulation
Other considerations for use in acute pain

Relatively cardiac/hemodynamically stable - useful for trauma, unstable patients 
Less respiratory depression then high dose opiates

title: 2015B Question 2
text:
Examiner Comments

15% of candidates achieved a pass in this question
This question consisted of three components and all components required answering to pass. The better candidates listed the correct components of soda lime and showed a basic understanding of chemistry with correct formulae and knowledge of how pH indicators work. The chemical reactions in soda lime were not asked for nor the anatomy of the circle system. Many candidates outlined the hazards of soda lime but not how to reduce these hazards. The factors which increase the production of Compound A and CO were not awarded points. The question asked for factors which decreased the production of Compound A and CO. There was confusion regarding fresh gas flow in relation to CO production; high fresh gas flow desiccates soda lime predisposing to CO production but will also decrease the CO in a circuit when attached to a patient by flushing it out. Extra marks were awarded for understanding the role of silica and the importance of particle size in soda lime.

title: 2015B Question 2
text:

    Passing Standard

Passing Standard
Soda lime is a product used for absorbing CO2 from a closed or semi closed anaesthetic circuit.
It includes:
Ca(OH)2
NaOH
H2O 
pH indicator and silica
CO2 and Soda Lime undergo the following reaction to form CaCO3 and H20:
CO2 + H20 → H2CO3
H2CO3 + 2NaOH → Na2CO3 + 2H2O + Heat 
Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 → CaCO3 + 2NaOH 
General Hazards

Failure due to depletion → CO2 accumulation 
↑Resistance to gas flow 
↑Heat → all reaction exothermic can cause injury, ↑risk with sodalite as high heat 
Risk of Spill / dust inhalation and injury to eyes/lungs/skin 
Risk of circuit leak

Hazard Reduction: 

Use a well-sealed well-insulated canister. 
Change when depleted.
PPE and care with changing product 
Circuit test after absorber change

Specific Hazards:
Compound A
Production of Compound A with sevoflurane, primarily with Baralyme and Soda lime. Risk ↑if low FGF rate, high Sevoflurane partial pressure. Nephrotoxic in rats but uncertain consequence in humans 
Address by using FGF >2l/min, limiting length of low flow anaesthesia
Carbon monoxide production
Production of carbon monoxide from absorbent and volatile agent. Risk increased by dry/desiccated absorbent, enflurane/desflurane > sevoflurane 
Address by ensuring gas flow turned off after each anaesthetic and particularly overnight/over weekend. Check absorbent before use.

title: 2015B Question 3
text:
Examiner Comments

9.1 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
The question assumed that the person is breathing spontaneously with the right side down. Candidates needed to discuss changes to ventilation, perfusion, compliance, and FRC in both lungs. These were best considered using separate heading. Perfusion and ventilation are both increased to the dependent lung by about 10%, with better V/Q matching as well. There is increased compliance in the dependent lung as the lung tissue is less expanded. The dependent lung corresponds more to west zone three, the non-dependent to west zone two.
Extra marks were awarded for: increased ventilation to the nondependent lung in anaesthetised/paralysed people, changes with open chest, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, blood gas changes, time constants, and more detailed information on the main points.
Many candidates spent a lot of time detailing V/Q relationships and west zones in the upright position, without relating this to the lateral position, making it difficult to gain marks. There was some confusion over what side was dependent in the right lateral position. Marks were not awarded for details of one lung ventilation, positioning of double lumen tubes, surgical indications, risks/description of the right lateral position, and detailed descriptions of dead-space and shunt.
Other issues were: failure to relate the answer to the right or left lung, being imprecise when talking about compliance changes, repeating the same point multiple times, and that healthy people become hypoxic lying on their right side. Finally endoscopy is generally not performed in the right lateral position.

title: 2015B Question 4
text:
Examiner Comments

58.3 % of candidates achieved a pass in this question
A pass mark in this question could be achieved by giving an accurate definition of both half life and context sensitive half time followed by some discussion of the concepts. With respect to half life, marks were gained for discussing it as an exponential process which is related directly to volume of distribution and inversely to clearance (t1./2 = 0.693 Vd/CL) and that it is best used when describing a single compartmental model. Those who talked about half life in a multi-compartmental model, gained points for accurately describing both distribution (ɑ) and elimination (ɞ) half lives, each with its own exponential curve. Discussion of the clinical utility of half life, in determining: time to steady state with intermittent dosing and; dosing interval, was also awarded points. Listing the half lives of drugs attracted no marks unless it was framed in a clinical context (e.g short distribution half life of propofol determines offset of effect after a bolus, rather than the longer elimination half life). When discussing context sensitive half time (CSHT), it was expected that the candidates would discuss a multi-compartmental model to help explain CSHT. Marks were given for discussing how the features of a drug’s pharmacokinetic profile e.g. volume of distribution, lipid solubility & clearance, would affect context sensitive half time. A well drawn graph used to support the discussion was often useful, but merely reproducing a graph with no explanation scored minimal points. Extra marks were given to those candidates who used CSHT to discuss which drugs are appropriate, or not, for infusions (both short and long) and how they are used in TCI modeling. Stating that both half life and CSHT did not necessarily correlate with the drugs duration of effect was rewarded. Common sources of error were poor definitions, especially for CSHT. A number of candidates provided no discussion of half life. There was significant confusion between half life and time constant. Many candidates listed a number of context sensitive half times for various drugs without discussing why the numbers occurred and this attracted minimal marks. Whilst a large number of candidates mentioned that fentanyl has a long context sensitive half time following a prolonged infusion, due to it sequestration in fat stores, very few people discussed the case for short infusions of fentanyl where the CSHT is relatively short due to distribution from the plasma in to fat.

Passing Standard
Half Life:
Half-life refers to the time taken for plasma concentration of a drug fall by 50% 

most relevant to single compartment model 
Exponential process related to volume of distribution and inversely proportion to clearance

T1/2 = 0.693xVd / Cl 
In  multi compartment model the t1/2 may refer to the distribution or terminal elimination half time 

T/2a Distribution half time 
T1/2b Elimination half time 


Context Sensitive Half Time (CSHT):
CHHT refers to the time taken for plasma drug concentration to fall by 50% of its value after cessation of an infusion, in context of the duration of the infusion.
For drugs described by single compartment models this is the half time, however all anaesthetic drugs are multi compartment 
CHST determinants:

duration of the infusion and therefore saturation of the peripheral compartments 
redistribution between peripheral and central compartments
clearance from the central compartment  

Differences between Half-life and CSHT
CHST describes the elimination kinetics from the central compartment in a multi compartment model. It has no fixed number and varies depending on infusion duration →‘context’

in short infusion times CSHT = t1/2a the redistribution half time
in longer infusions CSHT = t1/2b the terminal elimination half time 

Relevant Examples
Fentanyl Vs Remifentanil

Both fentanyl and remifentanil have rapid t1/2a times and redistribute rapidly. However fentanyl is far more lipophilic and so has larger volume of distribution.
Remifentanil has a small Vd and undergoes metabolism in tissue and plasma and so results is rapid clearance. 
Fentanyl redistributes from peripheral compartments which results in longer terminal elimination time / CSHT.
